subsections.heading: Temperature
subsections.html:
Both directionsK = °C + 273 °C = K − 273K = temperature in kelvin · °C = temperature in degrees Celsius · absolute zero is 0 K = −273 °C

Absolute zero is −273 °C, or 0 K. It is the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy and stop moving. In both gas law equations the temperature must be in kelvin — this is the most common way to lose all the marks on an otherwise correct calculation.

equations.name: Both directions
equations.symbolKey: K = temperature in kelvin · °C = temperature in degrees Celsius · absolute zero is 0 K = −273 °C

subsections.heading: Particles — the exact wording
subsections.html:
StateArrangementMotion
SolidClose together / touching, in a regular pattern or latticeVibrate about fixed positions
LiquidClose together / touching, but randomly arrangedSlide, flow, or move past one another
GasFar apart, randomly arrangedMove quickly in all directions, at random

The liquid row is where marks die. The examiner on 2025 Q3b: "For motion, really needed to say slide / flow / move past / move around — something to suggest a degree of contact between particles."

"The particles move" scores nothing. "The particles move past each other" scores. One word.

Also from 2023: correct candidates on the solid-versus-liquid comparison "usually referred to liquids being incompressible" — a detail worth having.

subsections.heading: How a gas exerts pressure — learn this as four beats
subsections.html:
1. Gas molecules move rapidly and randomly in all directions.
  2. They collide with the walls of the container.
  3. Each collision changes the molecule's momentum, so the wall exerts a force on the molecule and the molecule exerts a force on the wall.
  4. Pressure is force per unit area, so the total force from many collisions over the wall's area gives the pressure.

Say "molecules" or "particles", never "they". Reference P = F ÷ A and use it in the sentence rather than writing it in the margin — the examiner refused the mark for the equation floating unattached.

One more line the specification asks for: because the molecules move randomly in every direction, the pressure at a point in a gas or a liquid at rest acts equally in all directions — not just downwards. That is why a bottle is crushed inwards from every side, and why depth alone fixes the pressure in a liquid.

subsections.heading: The two gas laws at particle level
subsections.html:
LawStatementWhy, in particles
Boyle's law
constant temperature		Pressure is inversely proportional to volumeSmaller volume means the same number of molecules hit a smaller area more often, so pressure rises
Pressure law
constant volume		Pressure is directly proportional to kelvin temperatureHigher temperature means higher average kinetic energy, so molecules move faster, hit the walls more often and harder

From 2025: "Temperature is directly proportional to kinetic energy in Kelvin (temperature is not kinetic energy)." The kelvin temperature of a gas is proportional to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. It is not the same thing as it.

subsections.heading: Specific heat capacity
subsections.html:
Definition: the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

Water's is 4200 J/kg °C — unusually high, which is why water heats slowly, cools slowly, and is used in central heating and cooling systems. A substance with a low SHC changes temperature by a lot for the same energy input. That is the whole answer to the 2024 "why does the air heat more than the water" question.

subsections.heading: Two practicals you must be able to describe
subsections.html:
Density of an irregular solid

  • Measure mass on a balance, in grams or kilograms
  • Part-fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume
  • Lower the object in fully; record the new volume
  • Volume of object = final volume − initial volume (displacement)
  • ρ = m ÷ V

If the object floats, hold it under with a thin pin or use a sinker. If it's soluble, use a liquid it doesn't dissolve in.

Specific heat capacity of water

  • Measure the mass of water using a balance
  • Record the starting temperature with a thermometer
  • Switch the heater on and start a stopwatch simultaneously
  • After a measured time, record the final temperature
  • Energy supplied = power × time; then c = ΔQ ÷ (m × ΔT)
  • Insulate the beaker with a lid and lagging to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings

The insulation point is almost always worth a mark, as is stating that some energy is lost to the surroundings so the measured value is higher than the true value.

questions.promptHtml: A sealed rigid steel can of gas is heated. The volume cannot change. Explain, at particle level, exactly why the pressure rises — and identify two separate reasons.
questions.answerHtml:
Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so they move faster. That produces two distinct effects, and good answers name both:

One: faster molecules cross the container more quickly, so they hit the walls more often — more collisions per second.

Two: each molecule now arrives with more momentum, so each collision exerts a larger force.

More frequent and harder collisions mean a greater total force on the same area, so by P = F ÷ A the pressure rises.

Most students give only the first reason. The second is where the extra mark lives.

questions.promptHtml: Ice, water and steam are all H₂O. When ice melts at 0 °C, energy is supplied but the temperature doesn't change. Where is the energy going?
questions.answerHtml:
Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles. During melting, the energy supplied is not increasing that — it is going into breaking the bonds between particles, overcoming the forces of attraction that hold them in a fixed lattice.

So the energy is being transferred to the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy. The particles gain freedom to move past each other, but not extra speed.

On a temperature–time graph this shows as a horizontal plateau. There is one at the melting point and a longer one at the boiling point — longer because boiling requires breaking all the remaining bonds rather than just loosening them.

questions.promptHtml:
Two identical beakers each receive 10,000 J of energy. One contains 1 kg of water (c = 4200), the other 1 kg of copper (c = 385).

Which gets hotter, and by how much? Then explain why saucepans are made of metal but filled with water.
questions.answerHtml:
Rearranging: ΔT = ΔQ ÷ (m × c).

Water: 10 000 ÷ (1 × 4200) = 2.4 °C

Copper: 10 000 ÷ (1 × 385) = 26 °C

The copper gets hotter by roughly eleven times as much, because its specific heat capacity is about eleven times smaller.

The saucepan: the metal has a low SHC so it heats up rapidly for little energy, transferring heat to the food quickly. The water has a high SHC so it holds a lot of energy and its temperature stays stable, cooking food evenly rather than scorching it.

This is the same reasoning as the 2024 question about air heating more than water. Low SHC means big temperature change.

questions.promptHtml: A sealed plastic bottle is closed at high altitude where the air pressure is low. On landing, it is crushed. Why? And why would a rigid glass bottle not be?
questions.answerHtml:
When sealed, the pressure inside equals the outside pressure at that altitude — low. Descending, the outside pressure rises, but the trapped air inside stays at the low pressure.

There is now a pressure difference, with greater pressure outside than inside. Pressure acting on the bottle's surface area produces a force pushing inwards, larger than the outward force from the air inside. The resultant inward force crushes the bottle.

A rigid glass bottle doesn't collapse because glass is strong enough to withstand that resultant force without deforming — but the pressure difference is still there.

The 2025 examiner: "If missed MP2 its because they didn't specify that it was force causing it to collapse — instead kept saying pressure difference. Some didn't specify where the greater pressure was."

So: name the pressure difference, say which side is greater, and say that it produces a force.

questions.promptHtml: Why do you need to convert to kelvin for the gas laws, but not for the specific heat capacity equation?
questions.answerHtml:
The gas laws involve ratios of temperature. Doubling the kelvin temperature genuinely doubles the average kinetic energy — because the kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, where kinetic energy is zero. Going from 10 °C to 20 °C is not doubling anything physically; it's 283 K to 293 K, a rise of about 3.5%.

The SHC equation uses ΔT, a change in temperature. A rise of 20 °C is a rise of 20 K — the two scales have identical interval sizes, so the difference is the same number either way.

Rule of thumb: absolute temperature needs kelvin, temperature change doesn't care. The 2023 examiner noted students converting ΔT to kelvin, which was harmless but unnecessary.

questions.promptHtml: A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, while a solid holds its shape. Yet the mark scheme insists that a liquid's particles are still closely packed. How can both be true?
questions.answerHtml:
Because flowing is about order, not about spacing.

In a solid the particles are closely packed and in a regular, fixed pattern, so each one vibrates about a fixed position and the shape is held.

In a liquid the particles are still touching — essentially as close together as before — but the regular pattern has broken down. They are randomly arranged, so they can slide past one another. Close together, but not locked in place.

The evidence is in the volumes. Melting ice changes its volume by only a few per cent, because the spacing barely changes. Boiling water expands it about 1600 times, because that is when the particles genuinely move far apart. If liquids were not closely packed, melting would cause a huge expansion too.

2023's examiner noted students "regularly lost the third mark by stating the opposite". Say closely packed and randomly arranged.

questions.promptHtml: A syringe of gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature, and the pressure doubles. A student explains: "the particles are squashed together so they move faster and hit the walls harder." Two parts of that are wrong. Which, and what is the correct explanation?
questions.answerHtml:
Wrong 1 — they do not move faster. The temperature is constant, and temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy. If the particles sped up, the temperature would have risen. It hasn't, so they haven't.

Wrong 2 — they do not hit harder. The force of each individual collision depends on how fast the particle is moving, which is unchanged.

What actually changes is how often they hit. The same number of particles now occupies half the space, so the walls are closer and each particle reaches a wall more frequently. More collisions per second on each square metre means a greater total force per unit area — which is a greater pressure.

Contrast with heating at constant volume: there the particles genuinely do speed up, so they hit both more often and harder. Two different laws, two different explanations, and the exam tests whether you know which is which.

Mock 2 calls "they move faster" here "a common and costly error".

questions.promptHtml: The pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool depends on the depth, but not on how wide the pool is. Why not — surely a wider pool holds far more water pressing down?
questions.answerHtml:
It does hold more water — but that extra weight is spread over a proportionally larger area of floor, so the force per unit area is unchanged.

Pressure is force ÷ area. Doubling the width of the pool doubles the weight of water and doubles the floor area at the same time, and the two cancel exactly.

You can see it in the equation: ΔP = h × g × ρ contains the depth, the gravitational field strength and the density — and no term for width, area or total volume at all. The only things that matter are how deep you are and what the liquid is made of.

The practical consequence: a dam's thickness is determined by the depth of the reservoir, not by how many kilometres of lake stretch out behind it.

questions.promptHtml: A student measuring the specific heat capacity of a metal block gets a value higher than the accepted one. Their arithmetic is correct. Explain why the method pushes the answer the wrong way — and why it is always too high rather than sometimes too low.
questions.answerHtml:
The calculation assumes all the electrical energy supplied went into the block. In reality some is transferred to the surroundings — through the air, the bench and the wires.

So the energy actually used to raise the block's temperature was less than the figure used in the sum. Since c = E ÷ (m × ΔT), an overstated E gives an overstated c.

Why always too high: because the error is one-directional. Energy always leaks out of a block that is hotter than the room — it never leaks in. So the measured temperature rise is always smaller than the supplied energy would suggest, and the calculated c is always too large.

How to reduce it: insulate the block with lagging, and keep the temperature rise modest so there is less time and less temperature difference for losses to occur.

This "suggest why" question is worth two marks and appears in both mocks. Naming the direction of the error and linking it to the equation is what earns them.

questions.promptHtml: You must convert to kelvin for the pressure–temperature gas law, but you must not convert for the specific heat capacity equation. Why the difference?
questions.answerHtml:
Because one uses a temperature and the other uses a temperature difference.

The gas law is a proportionality. P₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂ ÷ T₂ says pressure is proportional to temperature, and a proportionality only makes sense measured from a true zero. Celsius zero is arbitrary — it is about water freezing, not about particles stopping — so "twice 10 °C" means nothing physical. Kelvin zero is the point where molecular kinetic energy is essentially zero, so doubling the kelvin temperature really does double the average kinetic energy.

The SHC equation uses ΔT, a change. A rise of 20 degrees is the same size on both scales, because the two scales have identical-sized divisions and only differ in where they start. 20 °C of change is 20 K of change, so converting achieves nothing — and converting the two temperatures separately before subtracting also works, since the 273s cancel.

The rule: a single temperature in a proportionality needs kelvin. A temperature difference never does.

questions.promptHtml: Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C; copper's is 385 J/kg °C. Explain what this means physically, and give two everyday consequences.
questions.answerHtml:
It means one kilogram of water needs 4200 joules to warm by one degree, while one kilogram of copper needs only 385 — about eleven times less. Water is unusually resistant to changing its temperature.

Consequence 1 — coastal climates are milder. The sea absorbs enormous amounts of energy in summer while warming only slightly, then releases it slowly in winter. Places near large bodies of water have smaller temperature swings than places inland.

Consequence 2 — water is used as a coolant and in heating systems. Central heating pipes and car radiators carry water because it can pick up a great deal of energy from the boiler or engine without its own temperature shooting up, then release it elsewhere.

A third, if you want it: a copper saucepan heats up almost instantly on the hob while the water in it takes minutes — same energy going in, wildly different temperature rises.

The exam version of this is "the same energy is supplied to oil, which has a lower specific heat capacity — what happens?" The oil gets hotter, because less energy is needed per kilogram per degree.

questions.promptHtml:
A metal block has a mass of 1.35 kg and measures 5.0 cm × 6.0 cm × 10.0 cm.

Calculate its density in kg/m³. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Volume = 5.0 × 6.0 × 10.0 = 300 cm³ 1

Convert: 300 cm³ = 300 ÷ 1 000 000 = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ 1

ρ = m ÷ V = 1.35 ÷ 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ 1

= 4500 kg/m³ 1

1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³, not 100. Three dimensions, so the conversion factor is cubed. This is the single nastiest unit conversion in the syllabus.

markScheme.point: = 4500 kg/m³

questions.promptHtml:
Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 250 g of water from 18 °C to 88 °C. (3)
(c for water = 4200 J/kg °C)
questions.answerHtml:
250 g = 0.25 kg, and ΔT = 88 − 18 = 70 °C 1

ΔQ = m × c × ΔT = 0.25 × 4200 × 70 1

= 73 500 J, or 7.35 × 10⁴ J 1

Two conversions hidden in one line: grams to kilograms, and the temperature change rather than the final temperature. Both are on the examiner's list of repeat offences.

questions.promptHtml:
A gas occupies 250 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. It is compressed at constant temperature to 80 cm³.

Calculate the new pressure. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ 1

100 × 250 = p₂ × 80 1

p₂ = 25 000 ÷ 80 = 312.5 kPa, or 313 kPa to 3 s.f. 1

Units of volume and pressure don't need converting here because they appear on both sides and cancel — as long as you're consistent. That is only true for Boyle's law. It is never true for temperature.

markScheme.point: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂

questions.promptHtml:
A fixed mass of gas at constant volume is at 27 °C and a pressure of 150 kPa. It is heated to 127 °C.

Calculate the new pressure. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Convert both temperatures: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T₂ = 127 + 273 = 400 K 1

p₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂ ÷ T₂ 1

150 ÷ 300 = p₂ ÷ 400 1

p₂ = 0.5 × 400 = 200 kPa 1

Had you used Celsius you'd have got 150 × 127 ÷ 27 = 706 kPa. Wrong by a factor of three and a half.

markScheme.point: Convert both temperatures: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T₂ = 127 + 273 = 400 K
p₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂ ÷ T₂

questions.promptHtml: Describe the arrangement and motion of the particles in a gas, and explain how this causes the gas to exert pressure on the walls of its container. (5)
questions.answerHtml:
Particles are far apart and randomly arranged 1

They move quickly, in all directions, at random 1

The particles collide with the walls of the container 1

Each collision exerts a force on the wall 1

Pressure = force ÷ area, so many collisions over the wall area produce a pressure 1

Write "particles" or "molecules" every time. Not "they", not "it".

markScheme.point: Particles are far apart and randomly arranged
They move quickly, in all directions, at random
The particles collide with the walls of the container
Each collision exerts a force on the wall
Pressure = force ÷ area, so many collisions over the wall area produce a pressure

questions.promptHtml:
A swimming pool is 2.4 m deep. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg.

Calculate the pressure due to the water at the bottom of the pool. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
ΔP = h × g × ρ 1

= 2.4 × 10 × 1000 1

= 24 000 Pa, or 24 kPa 1

Note this is the pressure due to the water alone. The total pressure at the bottom also includes atmospheric pressure pushing down on the surface — read carefully which the question wants.

markScheme.point: ΔP = h × g × ρ
= 24 000 Pa, or 24 kPa

questions.promptHtml:
A student pours hot water into a metal container, and stands it in a plastic cup of cold water.

(a) Sketch how the temperature of each body of water varies with time. (3)
(b) Explain why the temperatures change, referring to types of thermal energy transfer. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Hot water curve falls, steeply at first then levelling 1. Cold water curve rises, steeply at first then levelling 1. The two curves approach and meet at a common final temperature, between the two starting values 1

(b)

  • Energy is transferred from the hotter water to the cooler water, because energy always flows from higher to lower temperature 1
  • Conduction through the metal container wall — particles vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles; metals conduct well because of free electrons 1
  • Convection within each body of water — warmer water is less dense, rises, cooler water sinks to replace it, setting up a current 1
  • The rate of transfer decreases as the temperature difference decreases, which is why both curves level off 1

The 2023 examiner noted answers where "the rationale behind their response is in the wrong order". Energy flows because of a temperature difference — say that first, then name the mechanisms.

markScheme.point: (a) Hot water curve falls, steeply at first then levelling . Cold water curve rises, steeply at first then levelling . The two curves approach and meet at a common final temperature, between the two starting values
Energy is transferred from the hotter water to the cooler water, because energy always flows from higher to lower temperature
Conduction through the metal container wall — particles vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles; metals conduct well because of free electrons
Convection within each body of water — warmer water is less dense, rises, cooler water sinks to replace it, setting up a current
The rate of transfer decreases as the temperature difference decreases, which is why both curves level off

questions.promptHtml:
A student determines the specific heat capacity of a metal block using an immersion heater of power 45 W.

Describe the investigation the student should carry out. (5)
questions.answerHtml:
Any five 11111

  • Measure the mass of the block using a balance
  • Insert the immersion heater and a thermometer into the holes in the block
  • Record the starting temperature
  • Switch on the heater and start the stopwatch at the same moment
  • After a measured time, switch off and record the highest temperature reached
  • Calculate the energy supplied using E = P × t
  • Calculate the specific heat capacity using c = E ÷ (m × ΔT)
  • Insulate the block with lagging to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings

Recording the highest temperature matters: the block keeps warming for a while after the heater is switched off, as energy spreads through it. Reading too early makes ΔT too small.

markScheme.point: Any five

questions.promptHtml:
The block in D8 has a mass of 0.80 kg. The heater runs for 4.0 minutes and the temperature rises by 28 °C.

(a) Calculate the energy supplied by the heater. (3)
(b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) E = P × t 1

t = 4.0 × 60 = 240 s 1

E = 45 × 240 = 10 800 J 1

(b) ΔQ = m × c × ΔT, so c = ΔQ ÷ (m × ΔT) 1

c = 10 800 ÷ (0.80 × 28) 1

= 480 J/kg °C (2 s.f.) 1

The minutes-to-seconds conversion is the whole of the first mark in (a). Mock 2's mark scheme puts it bluntly: using 4 instead of 240 gives an answer 60 times too small.

markScheme.point: (a) E = P × t
(b) ΔQ = m × c × ΔT, so c = ΔQ ÷ (m × ΔT)

questions.promptHtml:
A student investigates a small irregular stone.

(a) Describe how the student could find the volume of the stone using a measuring cylinder. (3)
(b) The stone has a mass of 94 g and a volume of 36 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³, giving your answer to 2 significant figures. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Part-fill the measuring cylinder with water and record the volume 1

Lower the stone in until it is fully submerged, using a thread if necessary 1

Record the new volume and subtract the first reading to find the volume of the stone 1

(b) ρ = m ÷ V 1

= 94 ÷ 36 = 2.611… 1

= 2.6 g/cm³ (2 s.f.) 1

The answer is demanded in g/cm³ and the data is in grams and cubic centimetres — so no conversion at all. Converting to kg/m³ here would be wrong.

In 2024 the final mark was awarded specifically for 2 significant figures. As the examiner put it, 2 s.f. is not 2 decimal places: 2.61 is three significant figures and does not score.

markScheme.point: (a) Part-fill the measuring cylinder with water and record the volume
Lower the stone in until it is fully submerged, using a thread if necessary
Record the new volume and subtract the first reading to find the volume of the stone
(b) ρ = m ÷ V

questions.promptHtml:
(a) Describe the arrangement of the particles in a solid and in a liquid. (3)
(b) Describe the motion of the particles in a solid and in a liquid. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Particles in a solid have a regular arrangement 1

Particles in a liquid have an irregular or random arrangement 1

Particles in both are closely packed 1

(b) In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions 1

In a liquid, particles slide or flow past one another 1

The third mark in (a) is the one the year group kept losing, by saying liquids are not closely packed. They are — what changes on melting is the regularity, not the spacing.

In (b), "move freely" was ignored. The examiners wanted slide, flow, or move past each other.

markScheme.point: (a) Particles in a solid have a regular arrangement
Particles in a liquid have an irregular or random arrangement
Particles in both are closely packed
(b) In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions
In a liquid, particles slide or flow past one another

questions.promptHtml:
A solid is heated steadily until it melts. Its temperature–time graph shows a horizontal section.

Explain what is happening to the particles during this horizontal section. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
The energy supplied is used to break the bonds, or overcome the forces of attraction, between the particles 1

rather than to increase their kinetic energy 1

so the temperature stays constant while the substance changes state 1

The trap is answering "the energy is being used to melt it", which restates the question rather than explaining it. All three marks are in what the energy does to the bonds and to the kinetic energy.

markScheme.point: The energy supplied is used to break the bonds, or overcome the forces of attraction, between the particles
rather than to increase their kinetic energy
so the temperature stays constant while the substance changes state

questions.promptHtml:
A gas in a sealed rigid container is at 12 °C.

(a) Convert this temperature to kelvin. (1)
(b) The gas is heated. Explain what happens to the energy of its molecules. (2)
(c) Explain why a temperature below −273 °C is not possible. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 12 + 273 = 285 K 1

(b) The energy of the molecules increases 1

Specifically their kinetic energy increases, so they move faster on average 1

(c) At −273 °C the molecules would have essentially no kinetic energy left 1

You cannot remove energy that is not there, so no lower temperature is possible — this is absolute zero 1

2025's examiner made the point that temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy — temperature is not itself kinetic energy. The kelvin temperature is what is proportional to it, which is exactly why the scale exists.

markScheme.point: (b) The energy of the molecules increases
Specifically their kinetic energy increases, so they move faster on average
(c) At −273 °C the molecules would have essentially no kinetic energy left
You cannot remove energy that is not there, so no lower temperature is possible — this is absolute zero

questions.promptHtml:
A sealed syringe contains 80 cm³ of air at a pressure of 100 kPa. The plunger is pushed in until the volume is 32 cm³. The temperature does not change.

(a) Calculate the new pressure. (3)
(b) Explain, in terms of the particles, why the pressure changed. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ 1

100 × 80 = P₂ × 32 1

P₂ = 8000 ÷ 32 = 250 kPa 1

(b) The same number of particles now occupies a smaller volume 1

so they collide with the walls more frequently, increasing the total force per unit area and therefore the pressure 1

The particles do not speed up and do not hit harder — the temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy is unchanged. Only the frequency of collisions increases. Mock 2 calls saying they move faster "a common and costly error".

markScheme.point: (a) P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
(b) The same number of particles now occupies a smaller volume
so they collide with the walls more frequently, increasing the total force per unit area and therefore the pressure

questions.promptHtml:
A fixed mass of gas in a sealed rigid container is at 300 K and a pressure of 180 kPa. It is heated to 375 K.

(a) Calculate the new pressure. (3)
(b) Explain, in terms of the particles, why the pressure changed. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) P₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂ ÷ T₂ 1

180 ÷ 300 = P₂ ÷ 375 1

P₂ = 0.6 × 375 = 225 kPa 1

(b) The higher temperature means the particles have greater average kinetic energy, so they move faster 1

so they collide with the walls both more often and harder, increasing the force per unit area 1

Compare this deliberately with D14. There the particles did not speed up; here they do. The difference is whether the temperature changed, and the exam tests whether you can tell the two apart.

The temperatures are already in kelvin here. If a question gives Celsius, convert before substituting — this equation is a proportionality and Celsius has no true zero.

markScheme.point: (a) P₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂ ÷ T₂
(b) The higher temperature means the particles have greater average kinetic energy, so they move faster
so they collide with the walls both more often and harder, increasing the force per unit area

questions.promptHtml:
A sealed empty plastic bottle is carried onto an aircraft at high altitude, where the cabin pressure is low. As the aircraft descends, the bottle is crushed inwards.

(a) Explain why the bottle is crushed. (2)
(b) Explain, in terms of molecules, how the air outside the bottle exerts a pressure on it. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The air pressure outside the bottle increases as the aircraft descends 1

The pressure inside is unchanged, so there is a resultant inward force on the walls of the bottle 1

(b) The molecules move quickly and randomly in all directions 1

They collide with the surface of the bottle, and each collision exerts a force on it 1

Pressure is force ÷ area, so these collisions over the surface produce a pressure 1

2025's examiner: the collision mark was only given if molecules or particles were named — "they hit the walls" scored nothing. And the pressure = force/area point had to be linked into the answer, not just written down. Make it a sentence that joins the collisions to the pressure.

markScheme.point: (a) The air pressure outside the bottle increases as the aircraft descends
The pressure inside is unchanged, so there is a resultant inward force on the walls of the bottle
(b) The molecules move quickly and randomly in all directions
They collide with the surface of the bottle, and each collision exerts a force on it
Pressure is force ÷ area, so these collisions over the surface produce a pressure

questions.promptHtml:
An urn heats 6.0 kg of water from 18 °C to 98 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C.

(a) Calculate the energy transferred to the water. (3)
(b) The heating element operates at 230 V and draws a current of 10 A. Calculate the time taken to supply this energy, assuming all of it reaches the water. (4)
(c) In practice the urn takes longer than this. Explain why. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) ΔT = 98 − 18 = 80 °C 1

ΔQ = 6.0 × 4200 × 80 1 = 2 016 000 J (2.016 × 10⁶ J) 1

(b) P = I × V = 10 × 230 1 = 2300 W 1

t = E ÷ P = 2 016 000 ÷ 2300 1 = 877 s, about 15 minutes 1

(c) Some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and to the urn itself 1

so not all the electrical energy reaches the water, and more time is needed to deliver the required energy to it 1

ΔT is a difference: 80, not 98. This is a favourite way to lose the first mark.

markScheme.point: t = E ÷ P = 2 016 000 ÷ 2300 = 877 s, about 15 minutes
(c) Some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and to the urn itself
so not all the electrical energy reaches the water, and more time is needed to deliver the required energy to it

questions.promptHtml:
A heater supplies 9.3 × 10⁵ J of energy to a tank of water, raising its temperature by 45 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C.

Calculate the mass of water in the tank. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
ΔQ = m × c × ΔT, so m = ΔQ ÷ (c × ΔT) 1

m = 9.3 × 10⁵ ÷ (4200 × 45) 1

= 4.9 kg (2 s.f.) 1

2025 asked exactly this, and the examiner noted that some students struggled to rearrange the equation for mass. Practise making each symbol the subject in turn — m = ΔQ ÷ (cΔT), c = ΔQ ÷ (mΔT), ΔT = ΔQ ÷ (mc) — until none of them needs thinking about.

markScheme.point: ΔQ = m × c × ΔT, so m = ΔQ ÷ (c × ΔT)

questions.promptHtml:
The same amount of energy is supplied to 2.0 kg of water and to 2.0 kg of cooking oil. Oil has a lower specific heat capacity than water.

State and explain what happens to the temperature of the oil compared with that of the water. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
The oil reaches a higher temperature 1

because a lower specific heat capacity means less energy is needed per kilogram for each degree of temperature rise, so the same energy produces a larger temperature change 1

Check the logic against something familiar: water's specific heat capacity is unusually high, which is why a saucepan gets scaldingly hot in seconds while the water in it takes minutes to boil.

markScheme.point: The oil reaches a higher temperature
because a lower specific heat capacity means less energy is needed per kilogram for each degree of temperature rise, so the same energy produces a larger temperature change

questions.promptHtml:
A diver descends to a depth of 24 m in sea water of density 1030 kg/m³. Take g = 10 N/kg.

(a) Calculate the pressure due to the water at that depth. (3)
(b) State what happens to the pressure on the diver as she descends further, and why. (2)
(c) The pressure acts on her mask, which has an area of 0.012 m². Calculate the force on the mask due to the water pressure. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) ΔP = h × g × ρ 1

= 24 × 10 × 1030 1 = 247 200 Pa, about 247 kPa 1

(b) The pressure increases 1

because there is a greater height of water above her pressing down 1

(c) P = F ÷ A, so F = P × A 1

= 247 200 × 0.012 1 = 2966 N, about 3000 N 1

Note that pressure in a liquid acts equally in all directions — it presses on the mask sideways just as hard as it presses down on her shoulders.

markScheme.point: (a) ΔP = h × g × ρ
(b) The pressure increases
because there is a greater height of water above her pressing down
(c) P = F ÷ A, so F = P × A

modules.title: Electrical Circuits
modules.standfirst: Every single past paper contains a circuit diagram to draw. It is four marks, it is entirely predictable, and the year group kept losing it on unclosed wires.

intel.html:
PaperWhat was asked
2023 Q4 (9)Draw a circuit to investigate a filament lamp, plot the I–V results, curve of best fit, improving the investigation
2024 Q4 (12)Add a voltmeter to a circuit, V = IR twice, LDR resistance against light intensity, explain why LDR voltage falls
2025 Q5 (12)Draw a circuit to investigate a diode, current at a junction, V = IR, compare series and parallel currents with calculations

The shape repeats almost exactly: draw a circuit (4 marks), state the formula (1 mark), do a calculation or two, then one harder comparison or explanation question at the end. The first five marks are free if you're drilled.

2025: "students dropped marks for not connecting wires, leaving gaps in circuit. Incorrect circuit symbol for variable resistor, often drawing thermistor."

And on the final part: "poorly answered throughout the year group... A number of students used 13 as the total resistance for circuit B. A combination of correct calculations along with working or explanation required for 4 marks. Calculation alone without comparison of values was insufficient for full marks."

subsections.html: The cheat sheet in the next section is what you reread the night before. This is where the rules come from, so that when you can't remember one you can rebuild it. Every heading below says where it was actually asked — nothing is here because it is interesting.

subsections.heading: Drawing the investigation circuit
subsections.html:
2023 Q4(a) · 2025 Q5(a) · Mock 1 Q5(a) — 4 marks on every paper

This is the most predictable four marks in the whole exam. The question changes component — filament lamp in 2023, diode in 2025, thermistor in the mock — but the circuit is always the same:

  • Cell, variable resistor, ammeter and the component all in series, in one closed loop
  • Voltmeter in parallel across the component only — not across anything else
  • Correct symbols throughout
  • Every wire joined — no gaps, no loose ends

The variable resistor is what makes the experiment work: turning it changes the voltage across the component so you can take a range of readings instead of one. Leave it out and there is no method, and you lose the mark.

The meters go where they do because of what they measure. An ammeter counts the charge flowing through something, so it has to be in the path — series. A voltmeter measures a difference between two points, so it has to touch both of them — parallel.

2025: "students dropped marks for not connecting wires, leaving gaps in circuit. Incorrect circuit symbol for variable resistor, often drawing thermistor."

Two checks before you move on. Trace the loop with your finger from one terminal of the cell back to the other — if your finger comes off the line, that's a mark. And check the variable resistor has a diagonal arrow through the rectangle; a line that hooks upward at the end is a thermistor.

subsections.heading: Charge, current and the junction rule
subsections.html:
Spec 2.14, 2.15, 2.17 · 2025 Q5(b)(i) · Q = It also appears in the static electricity questions

Current is the rate of flow of charge. Learn that wording — it is a one-mark definition and it comes up. "Rate of" means "per second", so:

Q = I × t
Q = charge in coulombs (C) · I = current in amperes (A) · t = time in seconds (s)

So one amp is one coulomb per second. A current of 3 A means three coulombs pass any point every second.

Charge cannot be created, destroyed or leak out of the wire, which gives you two rules for free:

  • In a single loop the current is the same everywhere. Whatever goes into a component comes out of it.
  • At a junction, current in = current out. If 0.90 A arrives and 0.35 A goes down one branch, the other branch carries 0.55 A.

Students write that a bulb "uses up the current". It doesn't — it uses up energy. Every electron that goes in comes out again. If you ever write that the current is smaller after a component, stop.

Also: current in a solid metal is a flow of negatively charged electrons. That exact phrase is worth a mark on its own.

subsections.heading: Voltage, and why the voltages add up
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20, 2.21 · 2024 Q4(b)(iii) — "voltages of two components in series add to the supply voltage"

Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge passed. That is the spec wording, and it means one volt is one joule per coulomb.

E = Q × V
E = energy transferred in joules (J) · Q = charge in coulombs (C) · V = voltage in volts (V)

A 6 V battery hands 6 joules to every coulomb it pushes round. A component with 2 V across it takes 2 joules back out of every coulomb that passes.

Which immediately explains the rule the 2024 paper tested. Follow one coulomb round a 9 V circuit with two components: the battery gives it 9 J, the first component takes 5 J (so 5 V across it), the second takes 4 J (so 4 V), and it arrives back at the battery with nothing left — because it is back where it started. 9 = 5 + 4. The voltages across components in series add up to the supply voltage, because energy is conserved.

The move this gives you

In 2024 the paper gave the supply as 1.5 V, had you calculate 0.57 V across one component, then asked for the voltage across the other. You do not calculate it — you subtract: 1.5 − 0.57 = 0.93 V. One mark for knowing the voltages add, one for the arithmetic.

Whenever you know the supply and all but one of the series voltages, the last one is free.

Current flows through a component. Voltage is always across it — never through it. A voltage is a difference between two points, which is why it is properly called potential difference. "The voltage through the resistor" can cost you the mark in an explain question.

subsections.heading: V = IR — the workhorse
subsections.html:
Spec 2.13 · used in every single circuits question across all three past papers and both mocks

V = I × R
V = voltage in volts (V) · I = current in amperes (A) · R = resistance in ohms (Ω)

Resistance is the opposition to the flow of current, measured in ohms. Physically it comes from the moving electrons colliding with the vibrating metal ions — which is also why a component carrying a current gets hot.

You will be asked to rearrange it in both directions, so be fluent: I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I.

Papers routinely award a mark simply for stating the formula before you use it — 2024 Q4(b)(i), 2025 Q5(b)(ii), mock-1 Q5(c)(i) and mock-2 Q3(b)(i) all did. Write the equation down every time, even when you can do the sum in your head. It is the easiest mark on the paper and it is thrown away constantly.

subsections.heading: Series: resistances add, voltage shares out
subsections.html:
Spec 2.19 · 2025 Q5(b)(iv) · Mock 2 Q3(b)

In series the current is the same through both components and the voltages add. That gives you the rule in one line: V = IR₁ + IR₂ = I(R₁ + R₂), so Rtotal = R₁ + R₂. Resistances in series simply add.

It also gives you something more useful. Since the same current passes through both, and V = IR, each component's share of the voltage matches its share of the resistance. Twice the resistance, twice the voltage.

Worked example — the standard series calculation

A 12 Ω and an 18 Ω resistor are in series with a 9.0 V battery.

1. Total resistance: 12 + 18 = 30 Ω

2. Current (supply voltage with total resistance): I = 9.0 ÷ 30 = 0.30 A, the same through both.

3. Each voltage (that current with each resistance): 0.30 × 12 = 3.6 V and 0.30 × 18 = 5.4 V

4. Check: 3.6 + 5.4 = 9.0 V ✓ — and the bigger resistor took the bigger share.

That check takes five seconds and catches nearly every slip. Do it every time.

Mock 2 ran this backwards: given the current and the fixed resistor, find its voltage, then get the thermistor's resistance from what's left. Same three moves, different starting point.

subsections.heading: Parallel: same voltage, currents add
subsections.html:
Spec 2.18, 2.17 · Mock 1 Q5(c)

In parallel the current reaches a junction and has a choice of routes. Two rules:

  • Every branch has the full supply voltage across it — each branch is its own complete path from one terminal to the other.
  • The branch currents add up to the current from the battery.

Which means adding a parallel branch makes the total resistance go down. You are not adding an obstacle to an existing path, you are opening a new one — like opening a second till in a supermarket. More gets through per second, which is exactly what lower resistance means.

The method that cannot go wrong

You are not required to know the reciprocal formula, and reaching for it is where marks are lost. One branch at a time:

  1. Every branch has the full supply voltage.
  2. Each branch's current on its own: I = V ÷ R.
  3. Add the branch currents for the battery current.
  4. Only if asked for total resistance: R = V ÷ Itotal, at the very end.

15 Ω and 10 Ω across 3.0 V: I₁ = 3.0 ÷ 15 = 0.20 A, I₂ = 3.0 ÷ 10 = 0.30 A, total = 0.50 A.

Sanity check: a parallel total is always smaller than the smallest branch. Here R = 3.0 ÷ 0.50 = 6.0 Ω, less than 10 Ω ✓.

In 2025 candidates gave 13 Ω as a parallel total — they had added the branches as if in series. The method above makes that impossible, because you never add resistances at all.

Domestic lighting is wired in parallel for three reasons worth knowing (spec 2.7): each lamp gets the full mains voltage so runs at full brightness; each can be switched independently; and one failing leaves the others' circuits complete.

subsections.heading: Comparing two circuits — the question that failed the year group
subsections.html:
2025 Q5(b)(iv) — "poorly answered throughout the year group"

This is the hardest routine question in the topic and it is worth learning as a procedure, because the marks are awarded for structure as much as for physics.

In 2025: circuit 1 had a 19 Ω component; circuit 2 had 19 Ω and 13 Ω in series. Which carries more current?

  1. Work out the total resistance of each. 19 Ω, and 19 + 13 = 32 Ω.
  2. Say which is larger. Circuit 2 has the greater resistance.
  3. Work out both currents. 2.9 ÷ 19 ≈ 0.15 A and 2.9 ÷ 32 ≈ 0.09 A.
  4. State the conclusion in words. The current in circuit 2 is smaller, because its total resistance is larger while the supply voltage is unchanged.

The examiner: "A combination of correct calculations along with working or explanation required for 4 marks. Calculation alone without comparison of values was insufficient for full marks."

The words compare, comment on and explain the difference all require a sentence. Numbers on their own cap you well below full marks, however right they are. Write the "so it is bigger/smaller, because…" line every time.

subsections.heading: LDR and thermistor — the consequence chain
subsections.html:
Spec 2.11 · 2024 Q4(c) · Mock 2 Q3(c)

Two components, and the same direction for both — which is the opposite of what people guess:

ComponentBehaviour
LDRMore light → lower resistance (and the relationship is a curve, not a straight line)
ThermistorHigher temperature → lower resistance

Put either in series with a fixed resistor and the exam asks what happens to a voltage or a current. It catches people because two things change at once in opposite directions, so applying V = IR to the sensor itself proves nothing — its R falls while I rises.

The chain that always works

Argue through the component whose resistance has not changed. Taking 2024's LDR as light increases:

  1. Light up → LDR resistance down
  2. Total resistance down → current up
  3. Fixed resistor: same R, bigger I → its voltage rises
  4. The two voltages still add to the fixed supply → the LDR's voltage falls

Mock 2 asked the thermistor version — warmed, so resistance falls, so total resistance falls, so the current increases. Identical chain.

Learn the four steps as a unit. Each one is typically a mark, and writing only the conclusion scores one of four.

subsections.heading: I–V graphs: the filament lamp and the diode
subsections.html:
Spec 2.9 · 2023 Q4(c)(ii) · Mock 1 Q5(b) · 2025 Q5 (diode)

ComponentShapeReason
Wire / fixed resistorStraight line through the originResistance constant, so current is proportional to voltage
Filament lampCurve through the origin, steep at first then flatteningCurrent heats the filament; ions vibrate more; more collisions; resistance rises, so each extra volt buys less extra current
DiodeNothing until a threshold, then rising steeply; nothing in reverseConducts in one direction only

The filament lamp explanation is worth three marks and the chain must be complete: current → temperature → ion vibration → collisions → resistance increases. Skipping a link loses a mark.

Getting resistance off the graph. Take the coordinates of the point and do R = V ÷ I. Do not take the gradient of a curve — gradient equals 1 ÷ R only for a straight line through the origin.

For the "how would you improve this" mark, 2023's mark scheme wanted "take more data at different voltages". Repeating readings and averaging also scores.

subsections.heading: Power, energy and fuses
subsections.html:
Spec 2.3, 2.4, 2.5 · Mock 1 Q7(b) uses E = IVt

P = I × V  and  E = I × V × t
P = power in watts (W) · E = energy transferred in joules (J) · I = current (A) · V = voltage (V) · t = time in seconds (s)

P = IV follows from the definitions: voltage is joules per coulomb, current is coulombs per second, so multiplying gives joules per second. Note E = IVt is the same thing as E = QV, since Q = It — use whichever the question gives you.

Fuses use the heating effect as protection: a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current gets too high. To choose one, find the normal current with I = P ÷ V, then take the next standard rating above it — above, so it doesn't blow in normal use; only just above, so it still acts on a fault.

Time must be in seconds and currents in amps. Questions give minutes and milliamps precisely because the conversion gets forgotten: 4 minutes is 240 s, 250 mA is 0.25 A. Two conversions in one question is normal.

The 2025 examiner on the static questions: "Very few used standard form — please use it!" Large or small answers are safer written as 2.76 × 10⁶ than as a row of zeros.

subsections.heading: Series and parallel — the four rules
subsections.html:
SeriesParallel
CurrentSame everywhereSplits between branches; total in = total out at a junction
VoltageShares out; adds to the supply voltageSame across every branch, equal to the supply
Total resistanceAdd them: R = R₁ + R₂Less than the smallest branch. Find each branch current and add.
Adding a componentIncreases total resistance, so current fallsDecreases total resistance, so total current rises

The parallel method that never goes wrong

You are not required to know the reciprocal formula at IGCSE. Do this instead:

  1. The voltage across every parallel branch equals the supply voltage.
  2. Work out each branch's current separately using I = V ÷ R.
  3. Add the branch currents to get the battery current.
  4. If you need total resistance, use R = V ÷ Itotal at the end.

The 2025 candidates who wrote "13 Ω is the total resistance" had added a parallel pair as though it were series. This method makes that impossible.

subsections.heading: Circuit symbols — the ones that get drawn wrong
subsections.html:
ComponentWhat it looks like
CellOne long thin line and one short thick line. A battery is two or more cells in a row.
Fixed resistorPlain rectangle
Variable resistorRectangle with a diagonal arrow through it
ThermistorRectangle with a line that turns up at the end — not the same as a variable resistor
LDRRectangle in a circle, with two arrows pointing in
DiodeTriangle pointing at a line, showing the direction current can flow
AmmeterCircle with A. Always in series with the component being measured.
VoltmeterCircle with V. Always in parallel across the component being measured.

The standard investigation circuit

Almost every "draw a circuit to investigate how current varies with voltage across X" wants the same thing:

  • Cell, variable resistor, ammeter and component X all in series in one closed loop
  • Voltmeter in parallel across component X only
  • Every wire joined — no gaps, no floating ends

The variable resistor is what lets you change the voltage across X to get a range of readings. If you omit it you lose a mark and the method makes no sense.

subsections.html:
ComponentGraph shapeWhy

subsections.heading: LDR and thermistor
subsections.html: LDR: as light intensity increases, resistance decreases. Thermistor: as temperature increases, resistance decreases. Both are used in sensing circuits — an LDR in a streetlight switch, a thermistor in a thermostat.

questions.promptHtml: Two bulbs are in series. Does the first one "use up" the current, leaving less for the second?
questions.answerHtml:
No. Current is the same at every point in a series circuit. Charge is conserved — electrons are not consumed, they circulate.

What does get used up is energy. Each bulb transfers energy from the charge passing through it, which is why the voltage drops across each one and the drops add up to the supply voltage.

The useful mental model: current is like the rate of water flow round a closed loop — the same everywhere. Voltage is like the pressure drop across each obstacle. Water isn't destroyed by a waterwheel; its energy is extracted.

questions.promptHtml: A 20 Ω and a 30 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Without calculating, is the total resistance more or less than 20 Ω? Explain why.
questions.answerHtml:
Less than 20 Ω — and this surprises people, because "adding a resistor" sounds like adding resistance.

Adding a parallel branch gives the current an extra route. More total current flows from the battery for the same voltage. Since R = V ÷ I, a larger current at the same voltage means a smaller total resistance.

Checking: 6 V across each gives 0.3 A and 0.2 A, total 0.5 A, so R = 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12 Ω. Less than either branch, as it must be.

Sanity check to use in the exam: a parallel combination is always less resistive than its smallest branch. If your answer isn't, you've made an error.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the I–V graph for a filament lamp curve, while the one for a fixed resistor stays straight? Both are made of metal.
questions.answerHtml:
Both obey the same physics — the difference is temperature.

A filament lamp is designed to get white hot. As the current rises, the filament's temperature rises sharply. The metal ions in the lattice vibrate with greater amplitude, so electrons collide with them more frequently, so resistance increases. Increasing resistance means the current rises less and less for each extra volt — hence the curve flattening.

A fixed resistor is designed to dissipate its heat and stay near room temperature, so its resistance stays effectively constant and the line stays straight.

This is why the 2023 question asked whether a straight line was appropriate for a metal. The answer: current is only directly proportional to voltage at constant temperature, and a filament lamp is precisely the case where that condition fails.

questions.promptHtml: An LDR is in series with a fixed resistor across a cell. The lights come on and the LDR's resistance falls. Explain what happens to the voltage across the LDR — and why it isn't obvious.
questions.answerHtml:
It's not obvious because two things change at once, in opposite directions.

Total resistance falls, so the current in the circuit increases. For the LDR, V = IR with I up but R down — so which wins?

Work it from the other component. The fixed resistor's resistance is unchanged, and the current through it has increased, so its voltage rises. The two voltages must still add to the supply voltage, which is fixed. So the voltage across the LDR must fall.

The general principle: in a series pair, the component with the larger share of the resistance takes the larger share of the voltage. As the LDR's share of total resistance drops, so does its share of the voltage.

questions.promptHtml: In 2024 the paper gave a supply of 1.5 V, had candidates calculate 0.57 V across one component, then asked for the voltage across the other component in series with it. Many tried to calculate it from scratch. What should they have done, and why does it work?
questions.answerHtml:
Subtract: 1.5 − 0.57 = 0.93 V. No calculation from resistances is needed at all.

It works because the voltages across components in series must add up to the supply voltage. Each coulomb of charge is given 1.5 J by the supply and must spend all of it before returning — so if one component takes 0.57 J per coulomb, the other must take the remaining 0.93 J.

The mark scheme gave one mark for stating that the series voltages add to the supply, and one for the arithmetic.

Generalise it: whenever you know the supply voltage and all but one of the series voltages, the last one is free. Look for that before starting a longer route — it is quicker and it is what is being tested.

questions.promptHtml: A 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor are in series. Without doing a full calculation, which one has the larger voltage across it, and by what factor?
questions.answerHtml:
The 4 Ω resistor, and it has twice the voltage of the 2 Ω one.

The reasoning takes one line. In series the same current flows through both. Since V = IR and I is common to both, the voltage across each is directly proportional to its resistance. Twice the resistance, twice the voltage.

So the supply voltage splits in the ratio 2 : 4, or 1 : 3 and 2 : 3 of the total. On a 6 V supply that is 2 V and 4 V.

Worth internalising: "share of the resistance = share of the voltage" turns most series questions into mental arithmetic, and it is the whole basis of the LDR and thermistor questions.

questions.promptHtml: An ammeter goes in series and a voltmeter goes in parallel. Rather than memorising that, what is it about what each one measures that forces the placement?
questions.answerHtml:
Ammeter — measures current, which is charge flowing through something. To count what passes through a component, the meter has to be in the same path, so that all of that current goes through the meter too. That means in series with it.

Voltmeter — measures voltage, which is a difference between two points. A difference cannot be measured at one place; the meter has to be connected to both points at once. That means in parallel, across the component.

This is also why the language differs: current through, voltage across. The preposition tells you where the meter goes.

Mock 2 asked exactly this: add an instrument to measure the current, and state where it must be placed. One mark for "ammeter", one for "in series".

questions.promptHtml: A student measures a filament lamp and finds V = 3.0 V when I = 0.50 A. They then read the gradient of their curved I–V graph at that point and get a different value for the resistance. Which is right, and why do they disagree?
questions.answerHtml:
The R = V ÷ I calculation is right: 3.0 ÷ 0.50 = 6.0 Ω. The gradient is not the resistance here.

R = V ÷ I is the definition of resistance, so it works at any point on any graph for any component. It uses the coordinates of the point — how far across, how far up.

The gradient tells you something different: how much the current changes for a small change in voltage. Gradient equals 1 ÷ R only when the graph is a straight line through the origin, because only then is the ratio V : I the same as the rate of change.

A filament lamp's graph is curved precisely because its resistance is not constant, so the two numbers must disagree — and only the point calculation means anything.

The exam-safe rule: to get resistance from a graph, read off a point and divide. Never measure a gradient on a curve.

questions.promptHtml: Domestic lighting is wired in parallel rather than in series. Give three separate reasons why.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Every lamp gets the full mains voltage. In parallel the voltage across each branch equals the supply, so every lamp runs at its designed brightness. In series they would share the voltage out, so the more lamps you added, the dimmer they would all become.

2. Each can be switched independently. Each branch can have its own switch that breaks only that branch. In series, one switch would control everything.

3. One lamp failing does not affect the others. A blown filament breaks its own branch only; the other branches are still complete loops. In series, one failure opens the single loop and the whole house goes dark — which is exactly how old Christmas tree lights behaved.

The question is usually worth three marks and expects three distinct points, so don't write the same idea three ways.

questions.promptHtml: "A battery supplies a constant current." Is that statement right? Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
No. A battery supplies a roughly constant voltage — the current depends on what you connect to it.

A 9 V battery gives 9 joules to every coulomb it pushes round, whatever the circuit. But how many coulombs per second flow is set by the resistance: I = V ÷ R. Connect a 9 Ω resistor and you get 1 A; connect a 90 Ω resistor and you get 0.1 A. Same battery, ten times less current.

This is why adding components changes the current but not the supply voltage, and it is the assumption behind every calculation in this module: the supply voltage is the fixed thing, the current is the consequence.

questions.promptHtml: A thermistor is in series with a fixed resistor. Someone claims: "the thermistor gets hot, so its resistance goes up, so it takes more of the voltage." Two things in that sentence are wrong. Find them.
questions.answerHtml:
Error 1 — the direction is backwards. A thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises. This is the opposite of an ordinary metal resistor, and it is the single most common slip in the topic. Same for an LDR: more light means less resistance.

Error 2 — the conclusion doesn't follow anyway. Even if the resistance had risen, saying "so it takes more voltage" skips the reasoning. You have to argue through the other component: its resistance is unchanged, the current has changed, so V = IR gives its new voltage, and the two must still add to the supply.

Corrected: the thermistor heats up → its resistance falls → total resistance falls → current rises → the fixed resistor's voltage rises (unchanged R, larger I) → so the thermistor's voltage falls.

questions.promptHtml: Two identical bulbs are connected in parallel across a battery. A third identical bulb is now added in parallel with them. What happens to the current drawn from the battery, and to the brightness of the original two?
questions.answerHtml:
Current from the battery increases — by half as much again, since there are now three branches instead of two.

The original two are unchanged in brightness (assuming an ideal battery). Each branch still has the full supply voltage across it and the same resistance, so each still carries the same current and transfers energy at the same rate.

That is the point of parallel wiring, and it is why it is used for domestic lighting: adding a lamp does not dim the existing ones. Adding a branch does not take anything away from the branches already there — it just asks more of the battery.

Contrast with series: adding a third bulb in series would increase the total resistance, reduce the current, and make all three dimmer than the original two.

In reality a battery has some internal resistance, so a very large number of branches would eventually dim everything. That is not on this specification — the ideal answer above is the one being marked.

questions.promptHtml:
A student has a cell, a thermistor, a variable resistor, an ammeter, a voltmeter and connecting wires.

Draw a circuit diagram the student could use to investigate how the current in the thermistor varies with the voltage across it. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Cell, variable resistor, ammeter and thermistor all in series in one complete loop 1

Voltmeter connected in parallel across the thermistor only 1

All correct circuit symbols used, thermistor distinct from variable resistor 1

Circuit fully closed — every wire joined, no gaps 1

Before you put your pen down, trace the loop with your finger from one terminal of the cell all the way back to the other. If your finger comes off the line, you've lost a mark.

markScheme.point: Cell, variable resistor, ammeter and thermistor all in series in one complete loop

questions.promptHtml:
State the formula linking charge, current and time. (1)

A current of 250 mA flows for 4.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Q = I × t 1

250 mA = 0.25 A, and 4.0 minutes = 240 s 1

Q = 0.25 × 240 1

= 60 C 1

Two conversions. Milliamps to amps, and minutes to seconds. Both are standard bait.

markScheme.point: Q = I × t
250 mA = 0.25 A, and 4.0 minutes = 240 s

questions.promptHtml:
A 12 Ω resistor and an 18 Ω resistor are connected in series with a 9.0 V battery.

(a) Calculate the current in the circuit. (3)
(b) Calculate the voltage across the 18 Ω resistor. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Total resistance = 12 + 18 = 30 Ω 1

I = V ÷ R = 9.0 ÷ 30 1 = 0.30 A 1

(b) V = I × R = 0.30 × 18 1 = 5.4 V 1

Check: the other resistor takes 0.30 × 12 = 3.6 V, and 5.4 + 3.6 = 9.0 V. The voltages must add to the supply. Do this check every time — it costs five seconds and catches most errors.

markScheme.point: (a) Total resistance = 12 + 18 = 30 Ω

questions.promptHtml:
The same 12 Ω and 18 Ω resistors are now connected in parallel across the same 9.0 V battery.

Comment on the difference between the current supplied by the battery in this circuit and in the series circuit of D3. Use calculations to support your answer. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
In parallel, each resistor has the full 9.0 V across it 1

I₁ = 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A and I₂ = 9.0 ÷ 18 = 0.50 A 1

Total battery current = 0.75 + 0.50 = 1.25 A 1

This is larger than the series current of 0.30 A — about four times larger — because the parallel arrangement has a lower total resistance, giving the current additional paths 1

This is the exact question type the 2025 year group failed. The examiner: "Calculation alone without comparison of values was insufficient for full marks." The word comment or compare means you must write a sentence saying which is bigger and why. Numbers alone cap you at three marks.

markScheme.point: In parallel, each resistor has the full 9.0 V across it
Total battery current = 0.75 + 0.50 = 1.25 A
This is larger than the series current of 0.30 A — about four times larger — because the parallel arrangement has a lower total resistance, giving the current additional paths

questions.promptHtml:
A hairdryer is rated at 1800 W and runs from a 230 V supply.

(a) Calculate the current it draws. (3)
(b) Fuses are available rated at 3 A, 5 A and 13 A. State which should be fitted, and justify your choice. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) P = I × V, so I = P ÷ V 1

= 1800 ÷ 230 1 = 7.8 A (2 s.f.) 1

(b) The 13 A fuse 1

Because the fuse must be rated above the normal operating current, otherwise it would blow in normal use — but as close above it as available, so it still protects the appliance. A 5 A fuse would melt immediately. 1

markScheme.point: (a) P = I × V, so I = P ÷ V
(b) The 13 A fuse

Because the fuse must be rated above the normal operating current, otherwise it would blow in normal use — but as close above it as available, so it still protects the appliance. A 5 A fuse would melt immediately.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current through it increases. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
A larger current means more energy is transferred in the filament, so its temperature rises 1

The metal ions in the filament vibrate more vigorously 1

Electrons therefore collide with the ions more frequently, making it harder for charge to flow, so the resistance increases 1

Note the chain: current → temperature → vibration → collisions → resistance. Skipping a link loses a mark.

questions.promptHtml:
A 6.0 V battery drives a current of 0.40 A through a motor for 5.0 minutes.

Calculate the energy transferred. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
E = I × V × t 1

t = 5.0 × 60 = 300 s, so E = 0.40 × 6.0 × 300 1

= 720 J 1

You could also do it in two steps: Q = It = 120 C, then E = QV = 120 × 6.0 = 720 J. Same answer, and worth knowing in case a question gives you charge rather than time.

markScheme.point: E = I × V × t

questions.promptHtml:
State what is meant by current. (1)

State what is meant by voltage, and give the unit of voltage in terms of two other units. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
Current is the rate of flow of charge 1

Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge passed 1

One volt is one joule per coulomb 1

These are straight recall marks — spec points 2.14 and 2.20 — and they are given away almost every year. "Rate of flow of charge" must include the word charge: "rate of flow of electricity" does not score.

markScheme.point: Current is the rate of flow of charge
Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge passed
One volt is one joule per coulomb

questions.promptHtml:
A charge of 45 C passes through a lamp, transferring 540 J of energy.

(a) Calculate the voltage across the lamp. (3)
(b) The same lamp is left on for 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current in it. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) E = Q × V, so V = E ÷ Q 1

= 540 ÷ 45 1 = 12 V 1

(b) Q = I × t, so I = Q ÷ t 1

t = 3.0 × 60 = 180 s 1

I = 45 ÷ 180 = 0.25 A 1

Part (b) hands you the minutes-to-seconds conversion again. It is on nearly every paper.

markScheme.point: (a) E = Q × V, so V = E ÷ Q
(b) Q = I × t, so I = Q ÷ t

questions.promptHtml:
In the circuit below, the battery supplies a current of 0.90 A. This reaches a junction where it divides between two branches. The current in the first branch is 0.35 A.

(a) Determine the current in the second branch. (2)
(b) Explain, in terms of charge, why the two branch currents must add up to the current from the battery. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Current in = current out, so I₂ = 0.90 − 0.35 1 = 0.55 A 1

(b) Charge is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed at the junction, and none can accumulate there 1

So the charge arriving per second must equal the charge leaving per second, and since current is the rate of flow of charge, the currents must balance 1

Part (b) is spec point 2.17. The mark is for saying charge is conserved, not just restating that the currents add up — that is the thing being explained, so it cannot be the explanation.

(b) Charge is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed at the junction, and none can accumulate there
So the charge arriving per second must equal the charge leaving per second, and since current is the rate of flow of charge, the currents must balance

questions.promptHtml:
An LDR is connected in series with a 2.0 kΩ fixed resistor across a 6.0 V supply. A voltmeter is connected across the fixed resistor.

(a) In darkness, the LDR's resistance is 10 kΩ. Calculate the voltmeter reading. (4)
(b) The room lights are switched on. State and explain what happens to the voltmeter reading. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) In series, total resistance = 10 000 + 2 000 = 12 000 Ω 1

I = V ÷ R = 6.0 ÷ 12 000 1 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ A 1

V across the fixed resistor = I × R = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 2 000 = 1.0 V 1

(b) The voltmeter reading increases 1

Light falling on the LDR reduces its resistance, so the total resistance falls and the current increases 1

The fixed resistor's resistance is unchanged, so by V = IR a larger current means a larger voltage across it 1

Sanity check on (a): the LDR has five times the resistance of the fixed resistor, so it should take five sixths of the 6.0 V — 5.0 V — leaving 1.0 V. That agrees, and takes three seconds.

Watch the kΩ. 2.0 kΩ is 2 000 Ω. Working in kΩ throughout is fine too, as long as you then get milliamps and stay consistent.

(b) The voltmeter reading increases
