questions.promptHtml:
A thermistor is used in a circuit that switches on a cooling fan when a room gets too warm.

(a) Describe how the resistance of a thermistor varies with temperature. (1)
(b) The thermistor is in series with a fixed resistor. Explain why the voltage across the thermistor falls as the room warms up. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) As temperature increases, the resistance of the thermistor decreases 1

(b) The thermistor's resistance falls, so the total resistance of the circuit falls 1

Since the supply voltage is fixed, the current in the circuit increases 1

The fixed resistor's resistance is unchanged and the current through it has increased, so the voltage across the fixed resistor increases 1

The two voltages must add to the supply voltage, so the voltage across the thermistor must decrease 1

Do not try to answer this by applying V = IR to the thermistor itself — its R has gone down while I has gone up, so the argument is inconclusive and scores nothing. Always reason through the component whose resistance has not changed.

markScheme.point: (a) As temperature increases, the resistance of the thermistor decreases
(b) The thermistor's resistance falls, so the total resistance of the circuit falls
Since the supply voltage is fixed, the current in the circuit increases
The fixed resistor's resistance is unchanged and the current through it has increased, so the voltage across the fixed resistor increases
The two voltages must add to the supply voltage, so the voltage across the thermistor must decrease

questions.promptHtml:
A microwave oven is rated at 900 W and operates from a 230 V mains supply.

(a) Calculate the current in the oven when it is operating normally. (3)
(b) Fuses are available rated at 1 A, 3 A, 5 A and 13 A. State which fuse should be fitted and explain your choice. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) P = I × V, so I = P ÷ V 1

= 900 ÷ 230 1 = 3.9 A (2 s.f.) 1

(b) The 5 A fuse 1

It is rated above the normal operating current of 3.9 A, so it will not melt during normal use 1

It is the closest available rating above that current, so it will still melt and break the circuit if a fault causes the current to rise 1

The 3 A fuse would blow every time the oven was switched on. The 13 A fuse would allow more than three times the normal current before acting, so it would not protect the appliance. "Next one up" is the rule.

markScheme.point: (a) P = I × V, so I = P ÷ V
(b) The 5 A fuse
It is rated above the normal operating current of 3.9 A, so it will not melt during normal use
It is the closest available rating above that current, so it will still melt and break the circuit if a fault causes the current to rise

questions.promptHtml:
An electric heater draws 8.0 A from a 230 V supply and is left on for 25 minutes.

(a) Calculate the energy transferred, in joules. (3)
(b) Explain, in terms of electrons and ions, why the heating element gets hot. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) E = I × V × t 1

t = 25 × 60 = 1 500 s, so E = 8.0 × 230 × 1 500 1

= 2 760 000 J (2.76 × 10⁶ J, or 2 760 kJ) 1

(b) The current is a flow of electrons through the metal element 1

The electrons collide with the vibrating metal ions in the lattice 1

Each collision transfers energy to the ions, increasing their vibration — which is an increase in the internal energy and therefore the temperature of the element 1

Large answers like this are where powers of ten get dropped. Writing 2.76 × 10⁶ J is safer than counting zeros, and both are accepted.

markScheme.point: (a) E = I × V × t
(b) The current is a flow of electrons through the metal element
The electrons collide with the vibrating metal ions in the lattice
Each collision transfers energy to the ions, increasing their vibration — which is an increase in the internal energy and therefore the temperature of the element

questions.promptHtml:
Circuit A has a 10 Ω and a 15 Ω resistor in series with a 6.0 V battery. Circuit B has the same two resistors in parallel with the same battery.

Compare the current supplied by the battery in the two circuits. Use calculations to support your answer. (5)
questions.answerHtml:
Circuit A: total R = 10 + 15 = 25 Ω, so I = 6.0 ÷ 25 = 0.24 A 1

Circuit B: each resistor has the full 6.0 V across it 1

I₁ = 6.0 ÷ 10 = 0.60 A and I₂ = 6.0 ÷ 15 = 0.40 A, so total = 1.0 A 1

The current in circuit B is larger — about four times the current in circuit A 1

This is because the parallel arrangement gives the current two separate paths, so the total resistance is lower than in the series arrangement 1

This is the exact question the year group failed in 2025. The examiner: "A combination of correct calculations along with working or explanation required for 4 marks. Calculation alone without comparison of values was insufficient for full marks." The words compare and comment on require a sentence saying which is bigger and why. Numbers alone lose the last two marks. Also note 25 Ω is the series total — a candidate writing 25 Ω for the parallel total has made the classic error.

markScheme.point: Circuit A: total R = 10 + 15 = 25 Ω, so I = 6.0 ÷ 25 = 0.24 A
Circuit B: each resistor has the full 6.0 V across it
The current in circuit B is larger — about four times the current in circuit A
This is because the parallel arrangement gives the current two separate paths, so the total resistance is lower than in the series arrangement

questions.promptHtml:
A thermistor is connected in series with a 220 Ω fixed resistor and a 6.0 V battery.

(a) Name the instrument used to measure the current in the circuit, and state where it must be placed. (2)
(b) At room temperature the current is 12 mA. State the formula linking voltage, current and resistance, then calculate the voltage across the 220 Ω resistor. (4)
(c) Calculate the resistance of the thermistor. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) An ammeter 1, connected in series in the circuit 1

(b) V = I × R 1

12 mA = 0.012 A 1

V = 0.012 × 220 1 = 2.64 V 1

(c) Voltage across the thermistor = 6.0 − 2.64 = 3.36 V 1

R = V ÷ I = 3.36 ÷ 0.012 1 = 280 Ω 1

Part (c) is the series-voltages-add rule doing the work again: you get the thermistor's voltage by subtraction, not by another calculation. And the milliamps conversion in (b) is the standard trap.

markScheme.point: (a) An ammeter , connected in series in the circuit
(b) V = I × R
(c) Voltage across the thermistor = 6.0 − 2.64 = 3.36 V

questions.promptHtml: Sketch the shape of the I–V graph for (i) a fixed resistor and (ii) a filament lamp, on the same axes. Describe the difference and account for it. (5)
questions.answerHtml:
Fixed resistor: a straight line through the origin 1

Filament lamp: a curve through the origin, steep at first then becoming less steep as voltage increases 1

For the fixed resistor the current is directly proportional to the voltage, so its resistance is constant 1

For the lamp, increasing current raises the filament's temperature, so the ions vibrate more and electrons collide with them more frequently 1

The resistance therefore increases, so each additional volt produces a smaller increase in current — which is why the graph flattens 1

Both curves must pass through the origin: no voltage, no current. A common sketching error is starting the lamp curve away from the origin, which is the diode's behaviour, not the lamp's.

markScheme.point: Fixed resistor: a straight line through the origin
Filament lamp: a curve through the origin, steep at first then becoming less steep as voltage increases
For the fixed resistor the current is directly proportional to the voltage, so its resistance is constant
For the lamp, increasing current raises the filament's temperature, so the ions vibrate more and electrons collide with them more frequently
The resistance therefore increases, so each additional volt produces a smaller increase in current — which is why the graph flattens

questions.promptHtml: Describe the shape of the I–V characteristic for a diode, and explain what it shows about the diode's resistance. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
In the forward direction there is almost no current until a threshold voltage is reached (about 0.7 V) 1

Above that voltage the current rises very steeply 1

In the reverse direction the current is effectively zero at any voltage 1

So the diode has a very high resistance in reverse and below the threshold, and a very low resistance once conducting forwards — it allows current in one direction only 1

"Allows current in one direction only" is the phrase examiners look for. An LED behaves the same way and also emits light while conducting, which is why an LED can be used to show both the presence and the direction of a current.

markScheme.point: In the forward direction there is almost no current until a threshold voltage is reached (about 0.7 V)
Above that voltage the current rises very steeply
In the reverse direction the current is effectively zero at any voltage
So the diode has a very high resistance in reverse and below the threshold, and a very low resistance once conducting forwards — it allows current in one direction only

questions.promptHtml:
Full exam-style question. A student investigates how the current in a filament lamp depends on the voltage across it.

(a) Draw a circuit the student could use. (4)
(b) The lamp is rated 12 V, 24 W. Calculate its current at its rated voltage. (3)
(c) Calculate its resistance at that voltage. (2)
(d) At 3.0 V the student measures a current of 0.90 A. Calculate the resistance at 3.0 V and comment on the difference from part (c). (4)
(e) Suggest two improvements to the investigation. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Cell/battery, variable resistor, ammeter and lamp in series in a closed loop 1 · voltmeter in parallel across the lamp only 1 · correct symbols 1 · circuit fully closed with no gaps 1

(b) P = I × V, so I = P ÷ V 1 = 24 ÷ 12 1 = 2.0 A 1

(c) R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 2.0 1 = 6.0 Ω 1

(d) R = V ÷ I = 3.0 ÷ 0.90 1 = 3.3 Ω (2 s.f.) 1

This is lower than the resistance at 12 V 1

At the lower voltage the current is smaller, so the filament is cooler; the ions vibrate less, there are fewer collisions, and the resistance is lower 1

(e) Any two of: repeat each reading and take a mean 1 · take readings over a wider range of voltages / at more voltage values 1 · switch off between readings so the filament does not overheat · use meters with a finer scale division to reduce reading uncertainty

Part (d) is where the marks are won. The calculation alone gets you two of the four — the comparison and the temperature explanation are the other two, and this is precisely the pattern the examiner complained about in 2025.

markScheme.point: (a) Cell/battery, variable resistor, ammeter and lamp in series in a closed loop · voltmeter in parallel across the lamp only · correct symbols · circuit fully closed with no gaps
This is lower than the resistance at 12 V
At the lower voltage the current is smaller, so the filament is cooler; the ions vibrate less, there are fewer collisions, and the resistance is lower

(e) Any two of: repeat each reading and take a mean · take readings over a wider range of voltages / at more voltage values · switch off between readings so the filament does not overheat · use meters with a finer scale division to reduce reading uncertainty

questions.promptHtml:
Two resistors, 5.0 Ω and 20 Ω, are connected in series across a 10 V supply.

(a) Calculate the voltage across each resistor. (4)
(b) A third resistor is now added in series. State and explain the effect on the current in the circuit. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Total R = 5.0 + 20 = 25 Ω 1

I = 10 ÷ 25 = 0.40 A 1

V across 5.0 Ω = 0.40 × 5.0 = 2.0 V 1

V across 20 Ω = 0.40 × 20 = 8.0 V 1

(b) The current decreases 1

Adding a resistor in series increases the total resistance, and since the supply voltage is unchanged, I = V ÷ R gives a smaller current 1

Check on (a): 2.0 + 8.0 = 10 V ✓. And the 20 Ω resistor has four times the resistance so takes four times the voltage — 2 V and 8 V — which you could have written down without calculating the current at all.

markScheme.point: (a) Total R = 5.0 + 20 = 25 Ω
(b) The current decreases
Adding a resistor in series increases the total resistance, and since the supply voltage is unchanged, I = V ÷ R gives a smaller current

questions.promptHtml: Explain why the lights in a house are connected in parallel rather than in series. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Each lamp has the full supply voltage across it, so each operates at its normal brightness 1

Each lamp can be switched on and off independently of the others 1

If one lamp fails, the other branches are still complete circuits, so the remaining lamps stay on 1

Three marks means three genuinely different reasons. "They all stay on if one breaks" and "one breaking doesn't affect the others" are the same point written twice and will score once.

markScheme.point: Each lamp has the full supply voltage across it, so each operates at its normal brightness
Each lamp can be switched on and off independently of the others
If one lamp fails, the other branches are still complete circuits, so the remaining lamps stay on

questions.promptHtml:
A 3.0 V cell drives a current through a lamp. In 2.0 minutes, 36 C of charge passes through the lamp.

(a) Calculate the current. (2)
(b) Calculate the energy transferred by the lamp. (2)
(c) Calculate the power of the lamp. (2)
(d) The lamp is replaced by one of higher resistance. State the effect on the current and on the power. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) I = Q ÷ t = 36 ÷ 120 1 = 0.30 A 1

(b) E = Q × V = 36 × 3.0 1 = 108 J 1

(c) P = I × V = 0.30 × 3.0 = 0.90 W 1  (or P = E ÷ t = 108 ÷ 120 = 0.90 W) 1

(d) The current decreases, since I = V ÷ R with V fixed 1

The power decreases, since P = I × V and the current is smaller while the voltage is unchanged 1

Part (c) can be done two completely different ways, and they agree — a good habit when you have spare time at the end.

markScheme.point: (d) The current decreases, since I = V ÷ R with V fixed
The power decreases, since P = I × V and the current is smaller while the voltage is unchanged

modules.title: Waves and the EM Spectrum
modules.standfirst: Year 9 content that isn't revisited in Year 10, so it goes stale — and it's worth an eighth of the paper. Heavily recall-based, which makes it the fastest topic to bank marks in.

intel.html:
PaperWhat was asked
2023 Q3 (14)Meaning of 40 kHz, state v = fλ, calculate wavelength, calculate an echo time, three differences between sound and light
2024 Q2a (5)A shared property of all EM waves, a harmful effect of x-rays, transverse vs longitudinal
2025 Q1 (4)Name two missing parts of the EM spectrum, give a use of microwaves and of gamma rays
2025 Q4 (8)Particle motion in transverse vs longitudinal waves, explain the Doppler effect

Notice how much of this is straight recall. The EM spectrum in order, one use and one danger per band, and the transverse/longitudinal distinction account for most of it — and none of it requires understanding, only learning.

The uses are marked strictly. From 2025: "Did not allow 'microwaving food'" for a use of microwaves, and for gamma rays "Did not allow 'curing cancer', 'medicine', 'medical procedures/use', 'nukes'."

You must give the specific application from the specification. "Cooking" for microwaves. "Sterilising medical equipment" for gamma. Vague or colloquial answers score zero even when they're broadly true.

From 2023: "The students confused velocity for distance and did not quote the v=fλ equation... Sig Figs a problem for a lot of students."

subsections.html: A lot of this topic is straight recall — the spectrum in order, one use and one danger per band — and it is marked strictly, word by word. The rest is one equation used in three disguises. Every heading says where it was asked.

subsections.heading: What a wave is, and what it does not carry
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4

Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter. That sentence is the definition, and the second half is the part that earns marks.

Watch a duck on a pond as ripples pass: it bobs up and down and stays put. The water is not travelling towards the shore — each bit of water moves about its own position and passes the disturbance on. Same with sound: the air by your ear vibrates, but no air travels from the speaker to you.

So what moves along is the disturbance, carrying energy with it. This is why a wave can be enormously powerful without anything being thrown at you.

subsections.heading: Transverse and longitudinal
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2 · 2025 Q4(a) · 2024 Q2(a)(iii) · Mock 2 Q6(a) — asked in some form on every paper

The difference is the direction the particles vibrate, relative to the direction the wave travels.

Particles vibrateExamples
TransversePerpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of travelAll EM waves, water ripples, waves on a rope
LongitudinalParallel to the direction of travelSound, ultrasound

A longitudinal wave is a pattern of squashed regions and stretched regions — compressions and rarefactions — travelling along. Push and pull the end of a slinky and you can watch them move.

2024's mark scheme gives one mark just for mentioning vibrations or oscillations before you say anything about direction. Start your answer with the word "vibrate" and you have banked a mark.

Then use parallel and perpendicular. "Up and down" and "side to side" are not precise enough, because they depend on which way you have drawn the wave.

subsections.heading: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3, 3.24P · 2023 Q3(a) · Mock 1 Q4(a) — a 2-mark definition

  • Amplitude — the maximum displacement from the undisturbed position. Measured from the middle to a peak, not from peak to trough.
  • Wavelength (λ) — the distance for one complete wave, measured in metres. Peak to next peak works.
  • Frequency (f) — the number of complete waves passing a point per second, in hertz.
  • Period (T) — the time for one complete wave to pass, in seconds.
  • Wavefront — a line joining points on a wave that are all at the same stage, such as a line of crests.

"Explain what a frequency of 30 kHz means" — two marks

The mark scheme splits it in two, so say both halves: 30 000 complete waves 1 pass a point each second 1.

Saying only "30 000 hertz" scores nothing — that is restating the number, not explaining it. And remember the prefix: kHz means × 1000, and unit conversions like this are where the calculation marks go.

Worth knowing alongside: human hearing runs from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, so 30 kHz is ultrasound — above the range we can hear.

subsections.heading: v = f λ — and the mark for quoting it
subsections.html:
Spec 3.5, 3.7 · 2023 Q3(b) · 2025 Q4(c) · Mock 1 Q4(b)

v = f × λ
v = wave speed in metres/second (m/s) · f = frequency in hertz (Hz) · λ = wavelength in metres (m)

It works for every wave — sound, light, water, radio — which is why it appears three or four times a paper in different costumes.

2025's examiner: students "confused velocity for distance and did not quote v = fλ — quote the equation." There is a mark for writing it down before substituting, and it is regularly thrown away.

Same paper on significant figures: "a problem for a lot of students" — 5.5 × 10¹⁴ was rejected where 5.6 × 10¹⁴ was wanted. Carry the full number through your working and round only at the very end.

Watch the powers of ten. Light is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, wavelengths of light are around 10⁻⁷ m, and a slip of a single power costs the answer.

subsections.heading: Echoes and sonar — the factor of two
subsections.html:
2023 Q3(b)(iii) · Mock 1 Q4(c) — "the single most common error in echo and sonar problems"

A sonar pulse travels down to the sea bed and back again. The time you are given is for the whole round trip, so the distance you calculate from speed × time is twice the depth.

The method, with the halving made explicit

A pulse returns 0.16 s after being emitted. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. How deep is it?

1. Total distance travelled: 1500 × 0.16 = 240 m

2. That is there and back, so the depth = 240 ÷ 2 = 120 m

The factor of two is its own mark in both mark schemes. Write the words "there and back" in your working so the examiner can see you have used it.

The same applies in reverse: if you are given the depth and asked for the time, double the distance before dividing by the speed. In 2023, candidates who forgot scored 3 out of 4.

subsections.heading: Period, frequency and the oscilloscope
subsections.html:
Spec 3.6, 3.26P, 3.27P · Mock 2 Q6(c)

f = 1 ÷ T
f = frequency in hertz (Hz) · T = time period in seconds (s)

Frequency and period are two ways of saying the same thing. If one wave takes 0.005 s, then 200 fit into a second, so the frequency is 200 Hz.

A microphone connected to an oscilloscope turns a sound wave into a trace on a screen, letting you measure it. The horizontal axis is time, controlled by the time base setting — so many milliseconds per division.

Reading it, step by step

One complete wave spans 3 divisions; the time base is 2 ms per division.

1. Period: 3 × 2 ms = 6 ms = 0.006 s

2. Frequency: f = 1 ÷ 0.006 = 167 Hz

Convert milliseconds to seconds before taking the reciprocal. Forgetting gives an answer 1000 times out.

Note also what the trace shows: a taller wave means a larger amplitude, so a louder sound. A wave with more cycles across the screen means a higher frequency, so a higher pitch.

subsections.heading: Sound: pitch, loudness, and measuring its speed
subsections.html:
Spec 3.25P, 3.28P, 3.29P

Two straightforward links, and they are not interchangeable:

  • Pitch depends on the frequency of vibration of the source. Faster vibration, higher pitch.
  • Loudness depends on the amplitude of vibration of the source. Bigger vibration, louder sound.

To measure the speed of sound in air: stand a measured distance from a large flat wall, make a sharp sound, and time the delay before the echo returns. Speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time — the factor of two again, because the sound goes there and back. Repeat and average, and use a long distance so the time is big enough to measure reliably against your reaction time.

subsections.heading: The Doppler effect
subsections.html:
Spec 3.8 · 2025 Q4(b) · Mock 2 Q6(b) — 4 marks

When a source moves relative to you, the observed frequency and wavelength change. A siren sounds higher-pitched approaching and drops as it passes.

The reason is geometry, not physics of sound. As the source moves towards you it partly catches up with the waves it has already emitted, so they arrive bunched together — a shorter wavelength. Behind it, the waves are stretched out — a longer wavelength.

The four-mark answer, two marks for each direction:

  1. Approaching: the waves are squashed together, so the wavelength is shorter
  2. The wave speed is unchanged, so from v = fλ a shorter wavelength means a higher observed frequency — a higher pitch
  3. Receding: the waves are stretched out, so the wavelength is longer
  4. Again the speed is unchanged, so the observed frequency is lower — the pitch drops

Mock 2 is explicit: "do not write that the sound travels faster or slower. The speed is fixed by the air." The speed of sound depends on the medium, not on how fast the source is moving. What changes is the wavelength, and therefore the frequency you receive.

Note also that the source has not changed. The siren is emitting exactly the same note throughout — the driver hears no change at all.

subsections.heading: The electromagnetic spectrum
subsections.html:
Spec 3.10, 3.11 · 2025 Q1(a) · Mock 1 Q1(a)(c)

In order of increasing frequency and decreasing wavelength:

radio · microwave · infrared · visible · ultraviolet · X-ray · gamma

Within visible light, the same order runs red → orange → yellow → green → blue → indigo → violet: red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency, violet the shortest and highest.

What all EM waves have in common, which is a two-mark question in its own right:

  • All are transverse
  • All transfer energy
  • All travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
  • All can be reflected and refracted

Notice the pattern that makes the dangers memorable: the higher the frequency, the more energy each wave carries, and the more damaging it is. Radio waves pass through you harmlessly; gamma rays cause mutations.

subsections.heading: Uses and dangers — marked word for word
subsections.html:
Spec 3.12, 3.13 · 2025 Q1(b) · Mock 1 Q1(b) — "vague uses score zero"

This is pure recall and the strictest marking on the paper. Learn the specification's own wording:

BandUses (spec wording)Danger of excessive exposure
RadioBroadcasting and communications—
MicrowaveCooking, satellite transmissionsInternal heating of body tissue
InfraredHeaters, night vision equipmentSkin burns
VisibleOptical fibres, photography—
UltravioletFluorescent lampsDamage to surface cells, blindness
X-rayObserving internal structure, medical imagingCancer, cell mutation
GammaSterilising food and medical equipmentCancer, mutation

2025's examiner rejected a long list of near-misses. "Microwaving food" was not allowed as a use of microwaves — say cooking or heating food. For gamma, "curing cancer", "medicine" and "medical procedures" were all rejected — say sterilising equipment or treating cancer.

Mock 1 adds: "warming things up" is not "heaters". "Tanning" is not "fluorescent lamps."

The lesson is blunt. Do not paraphrase this table. Learn the phrases and write them.

Protective measures also appear: lead aprons and screens for X-rays, keeping exposure times short, sunscreen and sunglasses for ultraviolet, and handling gamma sources remotely from behind thick shielding.

subsections.heading: Reflection and refraction
subsections.html:
Spec 3.9

All waves can be reflected and refracted — sound as well as light.

Reflection bounces a wave off a surface; an echo is reflected sound. Refraction is the change of direction when a wave enters a different medium and changes speed.

The key to refraction questions: when a wave crosses into a new medium, its frequency stays the same — it is set by the source, and the waves cannot pile up at the boundary. So if the speed changes, from v = fλ the wavelength must change in proportion. Light entering water slows down, so its wavelength shortens.

Sound and light behave oppositely here, which is one of the standard "differences between sound and light" marks: light slows when it enters a denser medium, while sound speeds up — it travels faster in water than in air, and faster still in solids.

subsections.heading: Equations
subsections.html:
Wave equation — memorisev = f × λv = wave speed (m/s) · f = frequency (Hz — convert kHz to Hz first) · λ (lambda) = wavelength (m)
On the formula sheetf = 1 ÷ Tf = frequency (Hz) · T = time period, the time for one complete wave (s)

Speed of light and all EM waves in a vacuum: 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Speed of sound in air: roughly 340 m/s — questions usually give it.

equations.name: Wave equation
equations.symbolKey: v = wave speed (m/s) · f = frequency (Hz — convert kHz to Hz first) · λ (lambda) = wavelength (m)

equations.name: f = 1 ÷ T
equations.symbolKey: f = frequency (Hz) · T = time period, the time for one complete wave (s)

subsections.heading: Definitions
subsections.html:
TermSay this
AmplitudeThe maximum displacement of a point from its rest (equilibrium) position
WavelengthThe distance between a point on one wave and the same point on the next wave
FrequencyThe number of complete waves passing a point per second
Time periodThe time taken for one complete wave to pass a point
WavefrontA line joining all points on a wave that are in phase
TransverseVibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
LongitudinalVibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer

All waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter. That sentence is worth a mark on its own and appears constantly.

The number of complete waves passing a point per second
The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point

Vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer

subsections.heading: The EM spectrum
subsections.html:
In order of increasing frequency and decreasing wavelength:

Radio · Microwave · Infrared · Visible · Ultraviolet · X-ray · Gamma

Within visible light, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest. A mnemonic that works: Rich Men In Vegas Use eXpensive Gadgets.

BandUse — say exactly thisDanger
RadioBroadcasting and communications—
MicrowaveCooking, and satellite transmissionsInternal heating of body tissue
InfraredHeaters, and night vision equipmentSkin burns
VisibleOptical fibres, and photography—
UltravioletFluorescent lampsDamage to surface cells, skin cancer, blindness
X-rayObserving the internal structure of objects, including medical imagingMutation, cancer
GammaSterilising food and medical equipmentCancer, mutation

What all EM waves share: they are all transverse, they all transfer energy, they all travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s), and they can all be reflected and refracted.

equations.formula: Radio · Microwave · Infrared · Visible · Ultraviolet · X-ray · Gamma

subsections.heading: Sound
subsections.html:
• Sound is a longitudinal wave and requires a medium — it cannot travel through a vacuum.
  • Human hearing range: 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
  • Pitch depends on frequency. Higher frequency, higher pitch.
  • Loudness depends on amplitude. Larger amplitude, louder.
  • Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases — the opposite of light.

On an oscilloscope trace

The horizontal axis is time, set by the time base (e.g. 2 ms per division). Count the divisions for one complete wave to get the time period, then use f = 1 ÷ T.

A louder sound gives a taller trace. A higher-pitched sound gives waves squashed closer together.

subsections.heading: The Doppler effect
subsections.html:
When a source moves towards an observer, the waves ahead of it are squashed together: wavelength decreases and observed frequency increases. Moving away, the waves are stretched: wavelength increases, frequency decreases.

The wave speed itself does not change — it's set by the medium. Only the observed wavelength and frequency change. Saying "the waves speed up" loses the mark.

subsections.heading: Sound versus light — the standard comparison
subsections.html:
SoundLight
LongitudinalTransverse
Needs a mediumTravels through a vacuum
About 340 m/s in air3 × 10⁸ m/s
Faster in solids than gasesSlower in denser media
Not part of the EM spectrumPart of the EM spectrum

questions.promptHtml: You see lightning several seconds before you hear the thunder, even though both happen at the same instant. Estimate how far away a storm is if the gap is 6 seconds — and explain why you can ignore the travel time of the light.
questions.answerHtml:
Sound: distance = speed × time = 340 × 6 = about 2000 m, or 2 km.

Light covers that same 2 km in 2000 ÷ (3 × 10⁸) ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁶ s — about seven millionths of a second. Compared with 6 seconds, that is utterly negligible, so you can treat the flash as instantaneous.

The wider point: light is roughly 900,000 times faster than sound. Any question involving both — thunder, a starting pistol seen and heard, an echo timed with a stopwatch — you assume the light arrives instantly.

questions.promptHtml: A wave passes from air into water and slows down. Its frequency stays the same. What happens to its wavelength, and why must the frequency be unchanged?
questions.answerHtml:
From v = fλ, if v decreases and f is fixed, then λ must decrease. The wave gets shorter.

Why frequency can't change: frequency is set by the source. If 500 waves per second arrive at the boundary, 500 waves per second must leave it — otherwise waves would be piling up at the boundary or vanishing there, and neither happens. Waves are neither created nor destroyed at a boundary.

This is also the mechanism of refraction: the change of speed at the boundary is what bends the wave.

questions.promptHtml: An ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched as it approaches. Does the siren itself change? Explain what is physically happening to the waves.
questions.answerHtml:
The siren doesn't change at all. It emits exactly the same frequency throughout. What changes is what reaches your ear.

As the ambulance moves towards you, it partially catches up with the waves it has already emitted. Each successive wave is emitted from a position slightly closer to you than the last, so the waves bunch up. The distance between them — the wavelength — decreases.

The waves still travel at 340 m/s through the air. So with v fixed and λ smaller, v = fλ means the frequency you receive is higher, and you hear a higher pitch.

As it passes and recedes, the waves stretch out, wavelength increases and pitch drops — which is why the sound falls audibly at the moment of passing.

questions.promptHtml: Why is ultraviolet dangerous to skin while visible light and infrared, which reach you in far greater quantities from the Sun, are not — despite all three being electromagnetic waves?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the danger depends on frequency, not on quantity.

Higher frequency means each wave carries more energy. Infrared and visible light have relatively low frequencies — they deposit energy as heat, which the body handles routinely.

Ultraviolet sits above visible light in frequency, and carries enough energy per wave to be ionising: it can knock electrons off atoms and damage DNA in skin cells. Damaged DNA can cause mutations, which can lead to skin cancer. X-rays and gamma rays sit higher still and are correspondingly more dangerous.

The pattern to remember: moving right along the spectrum, frequency rises, energy per wave rises, and the biological danger shifts from heating to ionisation.

questions.promptHtml: A sonar question gives you the time for a pulse to return, and you calculate a distance of 240 m. Why is the answer to "how deep is the sea" not 240 m — and why is this described as the single most common error in the topic?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the pulse travelled down to the sea bed and back up again. The 240 m is the whole round trip, so the depth is 240 ÷ 2 = 120 m.

Why it catches so many people: the calculation itself is easy — speed × time — and it produces a confident-looking number. Nothing in the arithmetic reminds you that the journey was doubled. You have to spot it from the physical situation, and under time pressure that step gets skipped.

The habit that fixes it: write the words "there and back" in your working before you divide. Both mark schemes award the factor of two as its own mark, so making it visible earns it even if you then slip in the arithmetic.

It works in reverse too. If you are given the depth and asked for the time, double the distance first. In 2023, candidates who forgot scored 3 out of 4.

questions.promptHtml: A police car passes you with its siren on and the pitch drops. A student says the sound waves slow down as the car moves away. What is wrong with that, and what actually changes?
questions.answerHtml:
The speed of sound does not change at all. It is fixed by the medium — the air — and has nothing to do with how fast the source is moving. Mock 2's mark scheme says so explicitly.

What changes is the wavelength. As the car recedes, each wave is emitted from slightly further away than the last, so the waves arrive stretched out — a longer wavelength.

Then use v = fλ. The speed v is unchanged and the wavelength λ has increased, so the frequency f you receive must have decreased — and lower frequency means lower pitch.

The detail that proves the source hasn't changed: the driver hears no change whatsoever. The siren emits exactly the same note throughout. The effect exists only for an observer the source is moving relative to.

questions.promptHtml: Light slows down when it enters water, but sound speeds up when it enters water. Both are waves. Why do they behave in opposite ways?
questions.answerHtml:
Because they travel by completely different mechanisms.

Sound needs particles to carry it — it is passed on by particles bumping into their neighbours. The closer together and more strongly linked those particles are, the faster the disturbance is handed along. So sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases, and cannot travel through a vacuum at all.

Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium. It travels fastest in a vacuum, and anything it passes through only impedes it. So a denser medium slows light down.

What they share: in both cases the frequency is unchanged when the wave crosses the boundary — it is set by the source. So from v = fλ, whichever way the speed goes, the wavelength goes the same way.

This contrast is one of the standard marks in "give three differences between sound and light", along with longitudinal versus transverse and needing a medium versus not.

questions.promptHtml: The 2025 examiner refused "microwaving food" as a use of microwaves and "curing cancer" as a use of gamma rays. Both sound correct. Why were they rejected, and what should be written instead?
questions.answerHtml:
Because this part of the specification is assessed as recall of specific wording, and near-misses do not score.

"Microwaving food" uses the name of the wave to describe its own use — it is circular and says nothing about what is happening. The specification wording is cooking, or heating food. (The other listed use is satellite transmissions.)

"Curing cancer" overstates it and is not the specification's phrase. Gamma rays are used for sterilising food and medical equipment, and for treating cancer. "Medicine" and "medical procedures" were also rejected for being too vague to show you know anything specific.

Mock 1 adds two more: "warming things up" is not "heaters" for infrared, and "tanning" is not "fluorescent lamps" for ultraviolet.

What to do about it: this is the one part of the course where paraphrasing is actively punished. Learn the table of uses and dangers in the exact words and reproduce them. There are only about a dozen phrases and they are worth several marks a year.

questions.promptHtml: Amplitude is measured from the middle of the wave to a peak, not from peak to trough. Why does it matter which one you use, and what does amplitude correspond to for a sound?
questions.answerHtml:
Because measuring peak to trough gives you double the amplitude. Amplitude is defined as the maximum displacement from the undisturbed position — from the rest line to the top, not the full height of the wave.

On an oscilloscope trace this is an easy mark to throw away: the eye is drawn to the full vertical height of the wave, which is twice what is being asked for.

For a sound, amplitude means loudness. A larger amplitude of vibration at the source produces a louder sound. Frequency is separate and controls the pitch.

The two are independent, which is worth checking you believe: you can play the same note quietly or loudly (same frequency, different amplitude), and you can play a high note and a low note at the same volume (different frequency, same amplitude). On a screen, taller means louder and more-cycles-across means higher-pitched.

questions.promptHtml:
State the equation linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength. (1)

A radio station broadcasts at 98.4 MHz. Radio waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the wavelength. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
v = f × λ 1

98.4 MHz = 98.4 × 10⁶ Hz = 9.84 × 10⁷ Hz 1

λ = v ÷ f = (3.0 × 10⁸) ÷ (9.84 × 10⁷) 1

= 3.0487… 1 = 3.05 m to 3 s.f. 1

Mega means × 10⁶. Kilo means × 10³. Both appear constantly in wave questions and both are the difference between full marks and none.

markScheme.point: v = f × λ

questions.promptHtml:
An ultrasonic device emits a pulse at 45 kHz. The sound travels at 340 m/s.

(a) Explain what a frequency of 45 kHz means. (2)
(b) Calculate the wavelength. (3)
(c) The pulse reflects off a wall 3.4 m away and returns. Calculate the time between emission and detection. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 45 000 complete waves pass a point 1 every second 1

(b) λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 45 000 11 = 7.6 × 10⁻³ m 1

(c) Total distance = 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 m, because the pulse travels there and back 1

t = distance ÷ speed = 6.8 ÷ 340 1 = 0.020 s 1

The doubling in part (c) is the whole question. Any echo, sonar or ultrasound problem: the wave makes a round trip.

markScheme.point: (a) 45 000 complete waves pass a point every second
(c) Total distance = 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 m, because the pulse travels there and back
t = distance ÷ speed = 6.8 ÷ 340 = 0.020 s

questions.promptHtml: Describe the difference between the motion of the particles in a transverse wave and in a longitudinal wave. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
In a transverse wave the particles vibrate perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer 1

In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer 1

"Up and down" versus "side to side" doesn't score — it depends on which way the wave happens to be travelling. Use perpendicular and parallel, and always relative to the direction of energy transfer.

markScheme.point: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer
In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer

questions.promptHtml:
(a) Name the parts of the electromagnetic spectrum labelled X and Y in the sequence: radio — X — infrared — visible — Y — x-ray — gamma. (2)
(b) Give a use of infrared. (1)
(c) State a harmful effect of excessive exposure to microwaves. (1)
(d) State two properties all electromagnetic waves have in common. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) X = microwaves 1; Y = ultraviolet 1

(b) Heaters, or night vision equipment 1

(c) Internal heating of body tissue 1

(d) Any two: all transverse; all transfer energy; all travel at the same speed in a vacuum; all can be reflected and refracted 11

For (c), "it cooks you" won't do. The specification wording is internal heating of body tissue — use it.

markScheme.point: (a) X = microwaves ; Y = ultraviolet
(b) Heaters, or night vision equipment
(c) Internal heating of body tissue
(d) Any two: all transverse; all transfer energy; all travel at the same speed in a vacuum; all can be reflected and refracted

questions.promptHtml:
A train sounds its horn at a constant frequency while travelling towards a stationary observer.

Explain why the observer hears a higher frequency than the driver does. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
As the train moves towards the observer, each wave is emitted from a position closer to the observer than the previous one, so the waves bunch together 1

The wavelength reaching the observer is therefore shorter 1

The wave speed is unchanged, so from v = fλ a shorter wavelength means a higher observed frequency 1

Do not write that the sound travels faster. The speed of sound is a property of the air, not of the source.

markScheme.point: As the train moves towards the observer, each wave is emitted from a position closer to the observer than the previous one, so the waves bunch together
The wavelength reaching the observer is therefore shorter
The wave speed is unchanged, so from v = fλ a shorter wavelength means a higher observed frequency

questions.promptHtml:
An oscilloscope shows one complete wave spanning 4 divisions. The time base is set to 5 ms per division.

(a) Determine the time period. (2)
(b) Calculate the frequency. (2)
(c) State whether this sound is audible to a human, with a reason. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) T = 4 × 5 ms = 20 ms 1 = 0.020 s 1

(b) f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ 0.020 1 = 50 Hz 1

(c) Yes — 50 Hz lies within the human hearing range of 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz 1

markScheme.point: (c) Yes — 50 Hz lies within the human hearing range of 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz

questions.promptHtml: Give three differences between sound waves and light waves, other than differences in frequency and wavelength. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Any three 111:

  • Sound is longitudinal; light is transverse
  • Sound needs a medium; light can travel through a vacuum
  • Light travels far faster (3 × 10⁸ m/s against about 340 m/s in air)
  • Light is part of the electromagnetic spectrum; sound is not
  • Sound travels fastest in solids; light travels fastest in a vacuum

The question excludes frequency and wavelength, so don't waste an answer slot on them.

markScheme.point: Any three :

questions.promptHtml:
A ship uses sonar to measure the depth of the sea. It emits a pulse of sound at 25 kHz. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water.

(a) Explain what is meant by a frequency of 25 kHz. (2)
(b) State the formula linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength, and calculate the wavelength in sea water. (4)
(c) The pulse returns to the ship 0.24 s after it is emitted. Calculate the depth of the sea. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 25 000 complete waves 1 pass a point each second 1

(b) v = f × λ 1

25 kHz = 25 000 Hz 1

λ = 1500 ÷ 25 000 1 = 0.060 m 1

(c) Total distance = 1500 × 0.24 = 360 m 1

This is there and back 1

Depth = 360 ÷ 2 = 180 m 1

The factor of two in (c) is its own mark. Write "there and back" in your working. Failing to halve is "the single most common error in echo and sonar problems".

markScheme.point: (a) 25 000 complete waves pass a point each second
(b) v = f × λ
(c) Total distance = 1500 × 0.24 = 360 m
This is there and back

questions.promptHtml:
Green light has a wavelength of 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ m and travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

Calculate its frequency. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
v = f × λ 1

3.0 × 10⁸ = f × 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ 1

f = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ 1

= 5.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz (2 s.f.) 1

2025's examiner on this exact calculation: students "confused velocity for distance and did not quote v = fλ — quote the equation", and significant figures were "a problem for a lot of students" — an answer one digit out in the last place was rejected. Keep the full value in your calculator and round once, at the end.

markScheme.point: v = f × λ

questions.promptHtml:
A whale calls while swimming towards a second whale.

(a) Explain why the second whale hears a higher frequency than the whale that made the call. (3)
(b) State what happens to the frequency heard once the calling whale has passed and is swimming away. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) As the source moves towards the listener, the waves are squashed together, so the wavelength is shorter 1

The speed of the sound is unchanged, since it is fixed by the water 1

From v = f × λ, a shorter wavelength at the same speed means a higher frequency 1

(b) The frequency heard is lower — the waves are stretched out, so the wavelength is longer and the frequency falls 1

Do not write that the sound travels faster. "The speed is fixed by the [medium]." The only things that change are the wavelength and hence the observed frequency — the source itself emits an unchanging note throughout.

markScheme.point: (a) As the source moves towards the listener, the waves are squashed together, so the wavelength is shorter
The speed of the sound is unchanged, since it is fixed by the water
From v = f × λ, a shorter wavelength at the same speed means a higher frequency
(b) The frequency heard is lower — the waves are stretched out, so the wavelength is longer and the frequency falls

questions.promptHtml:
An oscilloscope displays a sound wave. One complete wave spans 5 divisions, and the time base is set to 4 ms per division.

(a) Determine the time period of the wave. (2)
(b) Calculate the frequency. (2)
(c) The sound is made louder without changing its pitch. Describe how the trace changes. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 5 × 4 ms = 20 ms 1 = 0.020 s 1

(b) f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ 0.020 1 = 50 Hz 1

(c) The wave becomes taller — a larger amplitude 1

The number of waves across the screen is unchanged, because the frequency and therefore the pitch is the same 1

Convert milliseconds to seconds before taking the reciprocal. Working in ms gives an answer 1000 times out.

markScheme.point: (c) The wave becomes taller — a larger amplitude
The number of waves across the screen is unchanged, because the frequency and therefore the pitch is the same

questions.promptHtml:
(a) State two properties that all electromagnetic waves have in common. (2)
(b) Name the parts of the electromagnetic spectrum missing from this sequence: radio · microwave · __A__ · visible light · __B__ · X-ray · gamma. (2)
(c) State how the frequency changes along the spectrum from radio to gamma. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Any two 11: all are transverse · all transfer energy · all travel at the same speed in a vacuum · all can be reflected and refracted

(b) A = infrared 1  ·  B = ultraviolet 1

(c) The frequency increases from radio to gamma (and the wavelength decreases) 1

The visible colours run in the same direction within their band: red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency, violet the shortest and highest.

markScheme.point: (a) Any two : all are transverse · all transfer energy · all travel at the same speed in a vacuum · all can be reflected and refracted
(b) A = infrared · B = ultraviolet
(c) The frequency increases from radio to gamma (and the wavelength decreases)

questions.promptHtml: Give one use and one danger of excessive exposure for each of: microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, and gamma rays. (8)
questions.answerHtml:
Microwaves — use: cooking or heating food, or satellite transmissions 1 · danger: internal heating of body tissue 1

Infrared — use: heaters, or night vision equipment 1 · danger: skin burns 1

Ultraviolet — use: fluorescent lamps 1 · danger: damage to surface cells, blindness 1

Gamma — use: sterilising food and medical equipment, or treating cancer 1 · danger: cancer, mutation 1

This is the strictest marking on the paper. 2025 rejected "microwaving food", "curing cancer", "medicine" and "medical procedures". Mock 1 rejected "warming things up" for infrared and "tanning" for ultraviolet. Reproduce the specification's phrases rather than your own.

markScheme.point: Microwaves — use: cooking or heating food, or satellite transmissions · danger: internal heating of body tissue
Infrared — use: heaters, or night vision equipment · danger: skin burns
Ultraviolet — use: fluorescent lamps · danger: damage to surface cells, blindness
Gamma — use: sterilising food and medical equipment, or treating cancer · danger: cancer, mutation

questions.promptHtml: Describe the difference between the motion of the particles in a transverse wave and in a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
In both, the particles vibrate or oscillate about a fixed position 1

In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of travel — for example light, or any electromagnetic wave 11

In a longitudinal wave the vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel — for example sound 1

2024's mark scheme gives a mark simply for mentioning vibrations or oscillations before any statement about direction. Open with that word. And use parallel and perpendicular, not "up and down" and "side to side", which depend on how the wave happens to be drawn.

markScheme.point: In both, the particles vibrate or oscillate about a fixed position
In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of travel — for example light, or any electromagnetic wave
In a longitudinal wave the vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel — for example sound

questions.promptHtml:
A student stands 85 m from a large wall, claps once, and hears the echo 0.50 s later.

(a) Calculate the speed of sound in air from these figures. (3)
(b) Suggest two ways the student could improve the accuracy of this measurement. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The sound travels there and back: distance = 2 × 85 = 170 m 1

speed = distance ÷ time = 170 ÷ 0.50 1

= 340 m/s 1

(b) Any two 11: repeat the measurement several times and take a mean · stand further from the wall so the time interval is longer and reaction-time error matters less · time several claps in succession and divide · use an electronic timing method rather than a stopwatch to remove reaction time

The factor of two appears here as a doubling rather than a halving, because you are given the one-way distance and the round-trip time. Always ask which of the two the question has handed you.

markScheme.point: (a) The sound travels there and back: distance = 2 × 85 = 170 m
speed = distance ÷ time = 170 ÷ 0.50

(b) Any two : repeat the measurement several times and take a mean · stand further from the wall so the time interval is longer and reaction-time error matters less · time several claps in succession and divide · use an electronic timing method rather than a stopwatch to remove reaction time

questions.promptHtml: Give three differences between a sound wave and a light wave, other than differences in their frequency and wavelength. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Any three 111:

  • Sound is longitudinal; light is transverse
  • Sound vibrations are along the direction of travel; light's are perpendicular to it
  • Light is part of the electromagnetic spectrum; sound is not
  • Light can travel through a vacuum; sound needs a medium and cannot
  • Light travels very much faster than sound
  • Light slows down in a denser medium; sound speeds up

The last one is the least well known and the most likely to separate answers. Sound is passed on by particles colliding, so closer-packed particles carry it faster; light is impeded by matter, so it is fastest in a vacuum.

markScheme.point: Any three :

questions.promptHtml:
A wave travels from air into glass. Its speed falls from 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s to 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. In air its wavelength is 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m.

(a) State what happens to the frequency of the wave, and why. (2)
(b) Calculate the wavelength of the wave in the glass. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The frequency is unchanged 1

It is determined by the source, and the waves cannot pile up or disappear at the boundary — the same number arrive each second as leave 1

(b) Find the frequency in air: f = v ÷ λ = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ 1 = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz 1

In the glass the frequency is the same, so λ = v ÷ f = 2.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 5.0 × 10¹⁴ 1

= 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m 1

Shortcut worth spotting: the speed fell to two thirds, and the frequency is fixed, so the wavelength must also fall to two thirds — 6.0 × ⅔ = 4.0. Useful as a check on the long method.

markScheme.point: (a) The frequency is unchanged
It is determined by the source, and the waves cannot pile up or disappear at the boundary — the same number arrive each second as leave
(b) Find the frequency in air: f = v ÷ λ = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
In the glass the frequency is the same, so λ = v ÷ f = 2.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 5.0 × 10¹⁴

questions.promptHtml:
Full exam-style question. An ultrasound scanner emits pulses at 2.5 MHz. Ultrasound travels at 1540 m/s in body tissue.

(a) State the frequency range of human hearing, and explain why 2.5 MHz is called ultrasound. (2)
(b) Calculate the wavelength of the pulse in body tissue. (4)
(c) A pulse reflects from a boundary 7.7 cm below the skin. Calculate the time before it returns. (4)
(d) State one reason ultrasound is preferred to X-rays for scanning an unborn baby. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Human hearing runs from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz 1

2.5 MHz is 2 500 000 Hz, far above 20 000 Hz, so it is above the range of human hearing 1

(b) v = f × λ 1, so λ = v ÷ f

2.5 MHz = 2.5 × 10⁶ Hz 1

λ = 1540 ÷ 2.5 × 10⁶ 1 = 6.2 × 10⁻⁴ m 1

(c) 7.7 cm = 0.077 m 1

The pulse travels there and back: distance = 2 × 0.077 = 0.154 m 1

time = distance ÷ speed = 0.154 ÷ 1540 1 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ s 1

(d) X-rays can cause cancer or cell mutation, while ultrasound does not damage cells 1

Three separate conversions in one question — MHz to Hz, cm to m, and the there-and-back doubling. This is exactly how the real papers build a long question.

markScheme.point: (a) Human hearing runs from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
2.5 MHz is 2 500 000 Hz, far above 20 000 Hz, so it is above the range of human hearing
(b) v = f × λ , so λ = v ÷ f
The pulse travels there and back: distance = 2 × 0.077 = 0.154 m
time = distance ÷ speed = 0.154 ÷ 1540 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ s
(d) X-rays can cause cancer or cell mutation, while ultrasound does not damage cells

modules.title: Static Electricity
modules.standfirst: A small topic that appears in every paper and produced the harshest examiner report in the pack. Almost entirely about saying one thing correctly: only electrons move.

intel.html:
PaperWhat was asked
2023 Q1 (6)Cloze passage on why cling film sticks to a plate — electrons, charge, attract and repel
2024 Q3 (12)Gold-leaf electroscope apparatus, charge sign, Q = It calculation, modifying apparatus to model safe aircraft refuelling
2025 Q2 (8)Why a pad charges on plastic but not on earthed metal, and describing an alternative experiment to show a pad is charged

The 2025 report on this question is the bluntest in the whole pack. "Overall this part not done well." Specifically:

"Some missed out on MP4 as they didn't state that the e-s went to earth and simply repeated the stem."

"Loads didn't know the name of the gold leaf electroscope – lost a mark if so as this is specifically mentioned in the spec."

"Any mention of magnets or electromagnetic force automatically lost all marks."

"Any mention of repulsion of the water stream lost the 2nd mark – too many think water is charged!!!"

And on the calculation: "too many thought that the energy 0.5mJ was the charge... Very few used standard form – please use it! Far too many POT errors too."

Read that list again before the exam. It is a near-complete specification of how to lose marks on this topic, written by the person who will mark it.
