subsections.html: A small topic — seven spec points — but it appears on every paper and the 2025 report on it is the bluntest in the pack: "Overall this part not done well." Almost all of the lost marks come from four specific wordings, which are flagged below.

subsections.heading: Only electrons move
subsections.html:
Spec 2.24P, 2.26P · 2023 Q1 · Mock 2 Q8(a) · Mock 1 Q2(a)

Everything in this topic is one idea: rubbing transfers electrons from one material to the other. That is the whole mechanism, and every explanation is a version of it.

An atom has a positive nucleus and negative electrons around it. The nucleus is locked in place; the outer electrons can be scraped off by friction. So:

  • The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged
  • The material that loses electrons is left positively charged

Note what that second line does not say. A positive charge is not created by adding anything — it is what remains when negatives are removed. Protons never move. If you find yourself writing that positive charges were transferred, that is wrong and it is a common way to lose the mark.

It also follows that the two objects always end up with equal and opposite charges, because every electron one gains is one the other lost. Charge is conserved.

The three-mark script for "explain how X becomes charged"

1. Friction (rubbing) between X and Y 1

2. Electrons are transferred from one to the other 1

3. X gains electrons and so becomes negatively charged, while Y is left positively charged 1

Name the direction the electrons move. "They become charged" without saying which way scores at most one.

subsections.heading: Conductors, insulators, and why only insulators stay charged
subsections.html:
Spec 2.22P, 2.23P · 2025 Q2(a)

Metals are conductors — they contain free electrons that can move through the material. Plastics are insulators — their electrons are bound to their atoms and cannot move.

This explains a result that otherwise looks arbitrary: rub a plastic rod and it charges; rub a metal rod held in your hand and nothing happens.

In both cases friction transfers electrons. The difference is what happens next. On the insulator the charge cannot move, so it stays where it was put. On the metal, the charge flows freely through the rod, through you, and away to earth — so no charge accumulates and there is nothing to detect.

2025 asked this as a car being polished: the pad charges on the plastic parts and not on the earthed metal ones, for exactly this reason.

subsections.heading: Forces between charges
subsections.html:
Spec 2.25P

Like charges repel. Unlike charges attract. Two negatives push apart, two positives push apart, a positive and a negative pull together.

2025's examiner: "Any mention of magnets or electromagnetic force automatically lost all marks."

This is not magnetism. Magnets have north and south poles and act on iron; charges are positive and negative and act on charged objects. The words "magnetic", "magnetised" and "attracted like a magnet" destroy an answer here, however well the rest is written.

subsections.heading: Earthing — and the mark almost everyone loses
subsections.html:
Spec 2.27P · 2024 Q3(c) · Mock 1 Q2(b)

Earthing means connecting a charged object to the ground with a conductor, so charge can flow away instead of building up.

The mark scheme is unusually specific here, in both papers. From 2025: "Some missed out on MP4 as they didn't state that the e-s went to earth and simply repeated the stem." And mock 1: "the electrons must be stated to flow to earth. 'It's earthed' restates the situation and scores nothing."

So the answer must say where the charge goes:

✗ "The aircraft is earthed, so it is safe."
✓ "Connect an earthing wire, so that electrons flow to earth and charge cannot build up."

The examiner is testing whether you understand earthing as a path for charge rather than as a magic word.

subsections.heading: Attracting things that are not charged
subsections.html:
Spec 2.26P · Mock 2 Q8(b) · 2023 Q1 — cling film

A charged rod attracts an uncharged stream of water, or scraps of paper, or sticks cling film to a plate. If the water is uncharged, why is there any force at all?

Because the charged rod rearranges the charges inside the neutral object without adding any:

  1. A negative rod is brought near. It repels the electrons in the water, pushing them to the far side of the stream.
  2. The near side is left with an induced positive charge; the far side is negative. The object is still neutral overall.
  3. The near side is closer to the rod than the far side, so the attraction beats the repulsion, and the stream bends towards the rod.

Mock 2: "any suggestion that the water is charged, or that it is repelled, loses marks. The department was emphatic about this." And from 2025: "Any mention of repulsion of the water stream lost the 2nd mark."

The stream is always attracted, whichever sign the rod carries — because the rod induces whichever charge it needs on the near side. Say induced, and say the stream stays uncharged overall.

subsections.heading: The gold-leaf electroscope
subsections.html:
Spec 2.23P · 2024 Q3(a) · Mock 2 Q8(c) — "loads didn't know the name"

A metal cap on a metal stem, with a thin gold leaf hinged against the stem, all inside a case. It detects charge.

Touch a charged rod on the cap and the leaf rises. The three-mark explanation:

  1. Charge from the rod spreads through the metal cap and stem to the leaf — the metal is a conductor 1
  2. The stem and the leaf now carry the same charge 1
  3. Like charges repel, so the leaf is pushed away from the stem and rises 1

The larger the charge, the further the leaf rises — so it measures as well as detects.

2025: "Loads didn't know the name of the gold leaf electroscope — lost a mark if so, as this is specifically mentioned in the spec." Learn the name. It is free marks for a piece of vocabulary.

subsections.heading: Dangers
subsections.html:
Spec 2.27P · 2024 Q3(c) · Mock 1 Q2(b)

The danger is always the same chain, and each link is a mark:

  1. Friction (fuel flowing through a pipe, a tanker driving along) transfers electrons, so charge builds up
  2. The charge builds until it is large enough that a spark jumps
  3. The spark can ignite the fuel vapour, causing a fire or explosion
  4. Prevented by earthing or bonding, so electrons flow to earth and charge cannot accumulate

Note that it is the vapour that ignites, not the liquid, and that the spark is the mechanism — "static electricity is dangerous" on its own explains nothing.

subsections.heading: Uses
subsections.html:
Spec 2.28P

Two named in the specification, both working by "unlike charges attract":

The photocopier. An image of the page is projected onto a charged plate. Where light falls the charge leaks away; the dark parts stay charged. Oppositely charged toner powder is attracted only to those charged regions, and is then pressed and heated onto the paper.

The inkjet printer. The ink is broken into tiny droplets which are given a charge as they leave the nozzle. They then pass between charged plates that deflect them by a controlled amount, steering each droplet to the right point on the paper.

subsections.heading: The calculations — and standard form
subsections.html:
2024 Q3(b) · 2025 Q2(b) · Mock 1 Q2(c) — "Very few used standard form — please use it!"

Two equations from the circuits topic reappear here, applied to very small charges:

Q = I × t
Q = charge in coulombs (C) · I = current in amperes (A) · t = time in seconds (s)

E = Q × V
E = energy transferred in joules (J) · Q = charge in coulombs (C) · V = voltage in volts (V)

Static charges are tiny — of the order of 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁹ C — so the numbers are always in powers of ten and the currents come out around 10⁻¹⁰ A.

2025: "Very few used standard form — please use it!" and far too many power-of-ten errors. Write 8.3 × 10⁻⁷ C, not 0.00000083 C — it is easier to get right and it is what the mark scheme expects.

Practise entering these on your calculator using the EXP or ×10ˣ key rather than typing "× 10 ^". Typing it out long-hand is where the stray zero creeps in.

The one rule everything follows from

Only electrons move. Protons never move.

An object becomes negatively charged by gaining electrons. An object becomes positively charged by losing electrons. There is no such thing as gaining or losing protons in electrostatics.

Every explanation in this topic is a sentence about which way electrons went.

subsections.heading: Charging by friction
subsections.html:
1. Two insulators are rubbed together.
  2. Friction transfers electrons from one to the other.
  3. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged.
  4. The material that loses electrons becomes positively charged, by an equal amount.

Note that the two charges are always equal and opposite — charge is conserved, it's only been moved.

subsections.heading: Forces between charges
subsections.html:
SituationForce
Like charges (both + or both −)Repel
Unlike charges (+ and −)Attract
Charged object and uncharged insulatorAttract — see below

Why a charged rod attracts uncharged paper: the rod's charge causes the electrons in the paper to shift slightly — repelled to the far side if the rod is negative, drawn to the near side if positive. The near face of the paper therefore carries an opposite charge to the rod and is attracted, while the more distant like charge is repelled less strongly. This is induced charge, and it's the only way a charged object attracts something neutral.

The famous demonstration is bending a stream of water with a charged rod. The 2025 examiner: "Any mention of repulsion of the water stream lost the 2nd mark – too many think water is charged!"

The water is neutral. It bends because charge is induced in it and it is attracted. It always bends towards the rod, whichever sign the rod carries.

subsections.heading: Conductors, insulators and earthing
subsections.html:
Conductor (metal)Insulator (plastic, rubber, glass)
ElectronsFree to move throughoutBound in place, cannot move through the material
Holds static charge?Not if it's earthed or handheld — charge flows away instantlyYes — charge stays where it's put

Earthing means connecting an object to the ground with a conductor. If the object is negatively charged, the excess electrons flow through the conductor to earth. If it is positively charged, electrons flow from earth onto the object. Either way the object ends up neutral.

This is where the 2025 marks were lost. It is not enough to write "it is earthed so the charge goes away". You must say which way the electrons flow, and that they flow to (or from) earth. The examiner refused the mark for answers that "simply repeated the stem".

subsections.heading: The gold-leaf electroscope
subsections.html:
Learn the name. It is in the specification and a mark was deducted for not knowing it.

How it works: a metal cap connects via a metal rod to a thin piece of gold leaf. Bring a charged object near, or touch the cap with it, and charge spreads through the metal to the rod and the leaf. The rod and leaf now carry the same charge, so they repel, and the leaf lifts away from the rod. The larger the charge, the further the leaf rises.

It's a detector of charge, and the deflection is the evidence.

subsections.heading: Dangers and uses
subsections.html:
Danger: refuelling an aircraft or tanker

  • Fuel flowing through the pipe rubs against it, transferring electrons — charge builds up by friction
  • If enough charge accumulates, a spark can jump between the pipe and the aircraft
  • The spark can ignite the fuel vapour, causing an explosion
  • Prevention: a bonding wire earths the aircraft and the fuel pipe, so electrons flow to earth and no charge builds up

Danger: lightning and touching a tap after walking on carpet

Same physics: friction charges an insulated object, charge builds, and it discharges suddenly through a conductor. A lightning conductor gives the charge a safe path to earth. Carpets with thin copper wires conduct the charge away as it forms.

Uses

Photocopier: a charged drum attracts oppositely charged toner powder, which is transferred to paper and fused by heat.

Inkjet printer: ink droplets are given a charge, then deflected by charged plates to steer them precisely onto the paper.

Electrostatic spray painting: paint droplets are given a charge and the object the opposite charge, so paint is attracted evenly and wraps round the object, wasting less.

questions.promptHtml: You rub a metal rod with a cloth while holding it in your hand. Nothing happens. You rub a plastic rod the same way and it charges. Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
Friction transfers electrons in both cases. The difference is what happens next.

The metal rod is a conductor, and you are holding it — your body and the ground provide a conducting path. The transferred electrons flow straight through the metal, through you, to earth. The rod cannot retain a charge, so it stays neutral.

The plastic rod is an insulator. Its electrons cannot move through the material, so the charge stays exactly where friction put it. The rod remains charged.

The test question: could you charge the metal rod? Yes — hold it by an insulating handle so there's no path to earth. That proves it's the earthing, not the metal.

questions.promptHtml: A positively charged rod is brought near a gold-leaf electroscope without touching it. The leaf rises. The rod is taken away without touching. The leaf falls again. Explain both.
questions.answerHtml:
Leaf rises: the positive rod attracts free electrons in the metal, drawing them up to the cap. This leaves the rod and leaf deficient in electrons, so both are positively charged. Like charges repel, so the leaf lifts away.

Leaf falls: the electroscope's total charge never changed — it was only redistributed. Remove the rod and the electrons flow back down, everything returns to neutral, and the leaf drops.

The contrast worth knowing: if you had touched the cap with the rod, electrons would have transferred permanently onto the rod. The electroscope would keep a positive charge and the leaf would stay up after the rod was removed. Induction is temporary; contact is permanent.

questions.promptHtml: Two objects are rubbed together. One ends up with a charge of −4 × 10⁻⁹ C. What is the charge on the other, and why can you be certain without knowing what the objects were?
questions.answerHtml:
+4 × 10⁻⁹ C — exactly equal in size, opposite in sign.

You can be certain because charge is conserved. Friction doesn't create charge, it moves electrons from one object to the other. Every electron gained by one is an electron lost by the other. If one gains a charge of −Q, the other must be left with +Q.

This is worth checking in any question giving both charges — if they aren't equal and opposite, either something else has been earthed or you've misread.

questions.promptHtml: Why is a spark dangerous during refuelling but not when you touch a door handle after walking across carpet — given both involve roughly similar amounts of charge?
questions.answerHtml:
The spark itself is much the same. The difference is entirely in what surrounds it.

A door handle sits in ordinary air. The spark releases a tiny amount of energy, you feel a sting, nothing else happens.

During refuelling, the air around the nozzle is full of fuel vapour, which is flammable. The spark supplies enough energy to ignite it, and the fuel supplies the rest — an explosion whose energy comes from the fuel, not the spark.

The exam-relevant point: when a question asks why static is dangerous, the answer is rarely the charge itself. It's that a spark acts as an ignition source in a flammable atmosphere, or that a large discharge can pass through a person.

questions.promptHtml: A charged rod attracts a thin stream of uncharged water. A student writes: "the water must have picked up a small charge, which the rod attracts." The mark scheme rejects this outright. What is actually happening?
questions.answerHtml:
The water stays uncharged overall. Nothing is transferred to it — the rod only rearranges the charge already inside it.

  1. Bring a negative rod close. It repels the electrons in the water, pushing them to the far side of the stream.
  2. The near side is left with an induced positive charge; the far side is negative. Total charge: still zero.
  3. The near side is closer to the rod, so its attraction is stronger than the far side's repulsion. Net result: the stream bends towards the rod.

The test that proves it is induction: the stream is attracted whichever sign the rod carries. A positive rod would pull electrons towards the near side instead, inducing a negative charge there — and again, attraction. If the water genuinely held a fixed charge, one sign of rod would repel it.

Mock 2: "any suggestion that the water is charged, or that it is repelled, loses marks. The department was emphatic about this." Use the word induced.

questions.promptHtml: Why can you never charge an object positively by adding positive charge to it? What actually happens instead, and what does this tell you about the other object involved?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the positive charge lives in the nucleus of each atom, and nuclei do not move. Friction can scrape off loosely held outer electrons; it cannot dislodge protons.

So a positive charge is always produced by removing electrons. The object is left with more protons than electrons, and the imbalance is what we call a positive charge.

What it tells you about the other object: those electrons went somewhere. Whatever was rubbed against it has gained exactly the electrons the first one lost, so it carries an equal and opposite negative charge.

That is why you can answer questions like "one object ends up with −4 × 10⁻⁹ C; what is on the other?" without knowing anything about the materials. It must be +4 × 10⁻⁹ C. Charge is conserved.

Writing that "positive charges were transferred" is a standard way to lose a mark. Only electrons move.

questions.promptHtml: "The aircraft is earthed, so refuelling is safe." The mark scheme gives this no credit at all, even though it is true. Why, and what would score?
questions.answerHtml:
Because it restates the situation rather than explaining it. The question has already told you there is an earthing wire; saying so back demonstrates nothing.

The examiners want evidence that you know what earthing physically does: it provides a conducting path along which electrons can flow to the ground, so charge cannot accumulate to the point where a spark jumps.

What scores: "An earthing wire connects the aircraft to the ground, so electrons flow to earth and charge does not build up. Without this, charge would accumulate until a spark jumped, which could ignite the fuel vapour and cause an explosion."

Both mark schemes flag this specifically. From 2025: "Some missed out on MP4 as they didn't state that the e-s went to earth and simply repeated the stem."

The general lesson: if your sentence could be written by someone who had only read the question, it will not score. Name the mechanism.

questions.promptHtml: A photocopier and an inkjet printer both rely on static electricity, but they use it in different ways. Explain how each works, and identify the single principle they share.
questions.answerHtml:
The shared principle: unlike charges attract, and a charge can be used to move small particles precisely.

Photocopier — charge is used to decide where powder sticks. An image of the page is projected onto a charged plate. Where light lands the charge leaks away; the dark regions of the image stay charged. Toner powder carrying the opposite charge is then attracted only to those still-charged areas, reproducing the image, and is pressed and heated onto the paper to fix it.

Inkjet printer — charge is used to steer droplets. The ink is broken into tiny droplets, each given a charge as it leaves the nozzle. They then pass between charged deflecting plates, which pull them sideways by an amount that depends on their charge — so each droplet can be aimed at exactly the right point on the page.

The difference in one line: the photocopier uses charge to control where the powder is attracted to; the printer uses it to control where a moving droplet lands.

questions.promptHtml:
A student rubs a balloon on a woollen jumper. The balloon becomes negatively charged.

(a) Explain how the balloon becomes negatively charged. (2)
(b) State the charge on the jumper and explain your answer. (2)
(c) The balloon then sticks to an uncharged wall. Explain why. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Friction transfers electrons 1; electrons move from the jumper to the balloon, so the balloon gains electrons 1

(b) Positive 1; the jumper has lost electrons, and charge is conserved so its charge is equal and opposite 1

(c) The negative charge on the balloon repels electrons in the wall's surface, pushing them deeper into the wall 1. The surface of the wall nearest the balloon is left positively charged — an induced charge 1. Unlike charges attract, so the balloon is attracted to the wall and held there 1

markScheme.point: (a) Friction transfers electrons ; electrons move from the jumper to the balloon, so the balloon gains electrons
(b) Positive ; the jumper has lost electrons, and charge is conserved so its charge is equal and opposite

(c) The negative charge on the balloon repels electrons in the wall's surface, pushing them deeper into the wall . The surface of the wall nearest the balloon is left positively charged — an induced charge . Unlike charges attract, so the balloon is attracted to the wall and held there

questions.promptHtml:
A charged object transfers a charge of 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ C to a metal can over a period of 15 s.

(a) State the formula linking charge, current and time. (1)
(b) Calculate the mean charging current. Give your answer in standard form. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Q = I × t 1

(b) I = Q ÷ t 1 = (6.0 × 10⁻⁸) ÷ 15 1 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ A 1

The examiner specifically asked for standard form to be used more. Don't write 0.000000004 A — you will make an error counting zeros, and it reads badly.

markScheme.point: (a) Q = I × t

questions.promptHtml:
A car is cleaned with a cloth pad. Parts of the car are plastic and parts are earthed metal.

Explain why the pad becomes charged when rubbing the plastic parts, but not when rubbing the earthed metal parts. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Rubbing transfers electrons between the pad and the surface by friction 1

Plastic is an insulator, so the electrons cannot move through it and the charge remains on the pad and the plastic 1

Metal is a conductor, so charge can flow through it 1

Because the metal is earthed, the electrons flow through the metal to earth, so no charge builds up 1

The fourth mark is the one the year group missed. You must say the electrons go to earth. Writing "it's earthed so it doesn't charge" restates the question and earns nothing.

markScheme.point: Rubbing transfers electrons between the pad and the surface by friction
Plastic is an insulator, so the electrons cannot move through it and the charge remains on the pad and the plastic
Metal is a conductor, so charge can flow through it
Because the metal is earthed, the electrons flow through the metal to earth, so no charge builds up

questions.promptHtml: Describe an experiment to demonstrate that an object is electrostatically charged. You may draw a diagram. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Bring the object close to the cap of a gold-leaf electroscope 1

The gold leaf rises away from the metal rod 1

Because charge spreads to the rod and leaf, which then carry like charges and repel 1

Acceptable alternative: hold the object near a thin stream of water from a tap; the stream bends towards the object because charge is induced in the neutral water and it is attracted.

Do not describe rubbing the object first — the question states it is already charged, and rubbing it would ruin the demonstration by confusing cause and effect. The examiner penalised this explicitly.

markScheme.point: Bring the object close to the cap of a gold-leaf electroscope
The gold leaf rises away from the metal rod
Because charge spreads to the rod and leaf, which then carry like charges and repel

questions.promptHtml: Explain the danger of static electricity when refuelling an aircraft, and describe how the danger is reduced. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Fuel flowing through the hose rubs against it, transferring electrons by friction so charge builds up 1

If enough charge accumulates, a spark can jump between the hose and the aircraft 1

The spark could ignite the fuel vapour, causing a fire or explosion 1

A bonding or earthing wire connects the aircraft to earth, so electrons flow to earth and charge cannot build up 1

If enough charge accumulates, a spark can jump between the hose and the aircraft

questions.promptHtml:
Workers assembling computer chips wear a bracelet connected by a wire to earth.

(a) State whether the bracelet should be made of copper, plastic or rubber, and give a reason. (2)
(b) Explain how this protects the computer chips. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Copper 1, because it is a conductor, so charge can flow through it to earth 1

(b) Any charge that builds up on the worker flows through the bracelet and wire to earth 1, so no charge can accumulate and discharge through a chip as a spark, which would damage it 1

markScheme.point: (a) Copper , because it is a conductor, so charge can flow through it to earth
(b) Any charge that builds up on the worker flows through the bracelet and wire to earth , so no charge can accumulate and discharge through a chip as a spark, which would damage it

questions.promptHtml:
A student rubs a polythene rod with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged.

(a) Explain, in terms of electrons, how the rod becomes negatively charged. (2)
(b) State the charge left on the cloth, and explain how you know. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Friction between the rod and the cloth transfers electrons 1

Electrons move from the cloth onto the rod, so the rod gains electrons and becomes negative 1

(b) The cloth is left positively charged 1

Every electron gained by the rod was lost by the cloth, so the cloth has a deficit of electrons — an equal and opposite charge 1

Say which way the electrons moved. "They become charged" without a direction scores at most one mark, and writing that positive charge moved onto the cloth is wrong — protons never move.

markScheme.point: (a) Friction between the rod and the cloth transfers electrons
Electrons move from the cloth onto the rod, so the rod gains electrons and becomes negative
(b) The cloth is left positively charged
Every electron gained by the rod was lost by the cloth, so the cloth has a deficit of electrons — an equal and opposite charge

questions.promptHtml:
A negatively charged rod is held near a thin stream of water flowing from a tap. The stream bends towards the rod, even though the water is uncharged.

Explain why. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
The negative rod repels the electrons in the water, pushing them to the far side of the stream 1

The near side of the stream is left with an induced positive charge 1

Unlike charges attract, and the near side is closer to the rod, so the stream is attracted and bends towards it 1

Mock 2: "any suggestion that the water is charged, or that it is repelled, loses marks." The stream remains uncharged overall — the charge within it is only rearranged. Use the word induced.

2025: "Any mention of magnets or electromagnetic force automatically lost all marks."

markScheme.point: The negative rod repels the electrons in the water, pushing them to the far side of the stream
The near side of the stream is left with an induced positive charge
Unlike charges attract, and the near side is closer to the rod, so the stream is attracted and bends towards it

(a) Describe and explain what happens to the gold leaf. (3)

(a) The leaf rises away from the metal stem 1

questions.promptHtml:
A charge of 7.2 × 10⁻⁷ C builds up on an object over a period of 45 seconds.

(a) State the formula linking charge, current and time. (1)
(b) Calculate the mean charging current. Give your answer in standard form. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Q = I × t 1

(b) I = Q ÷ t 1

= 7.2 × 10⁻⁷ ÷ 45 1

= 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ A 1

2025's examiner: "Very few used standard form — please use it!" Write 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ A, not 0.000000016 A. Enter these on your calculator with the EXP or ×10ˣ key rather than typing the power out, which is where stray zeros creep in.

questions.promptHtml:
A charged cleaning pad stores 0.008 J of energy at a voltage of 4500 V.

(a) State the formula linking energy transferred, charge and voltage. (1)
(b) Calculate the charge on the pad. Give your answer in standard form. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) E = Q × V 1

(b) Q = E ÷ V 1

= 0.008 ÷ 4500 1

= 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ C 1

2025 set this exact question with different numbers and reported widespread power-of-ten errors. Static charges come out in the 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁹ range — if your answer is a whole number of coulombs, something has gone wrong.

(b) Q = E ÷ V

questions.promptHtml:
A car is polished with a cloth pad. Some panels are plastic; others are earthed metal.

Explain why the pad becomes charged when rubbing the plastic panels but not when rubbing the earthed metal ones. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Plastic is an insulator and metal is a conductor 1

In both cases, friction transfers electrons between the pad and the panel 1

On the plastic the charge cannot move, so it remains where it was produced 1

On the earthed metal the charge flows away through the metal to earth, so none builds up 1

The mark for the metal case needs the charge to reach earth, not merely "the metal conducts". Say where it goes.

In both cases, friction transfers electrons between the pad and the panel
On the plastic the charge cannot move, so it remains where it was produced
On the earthed metal the charge flows away through the metal to earth, so none builds up

questions.promptHtml: Describe an experiment to demonstrate that a cleaning pad has become electrostatically charged. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
Bring the pad near a small uncharged insulator — pieces of paper, a thin stream of water from a tap, or someone's hair 1

The paper (or water, or hair) is attracted towards the pad, and this attraction demonstrates that the pad is charged 1

2025: it had to be an uncharged object being attracted. Rubbing something else first loses the mark, because the pad is already charged and does not need charging again. And "repulsion" was rejected unless linked to a gold-leaf electroscope — repulsion needs two known like charges, which a random object does not give you.

The paper (or water, or hair) is attracted towards the pad, and this attraction demonstrates that the pad is charged

subsections.html: Half-life is defined in two of the three past papers and calculated in all three. Get that definition exactly right and you have banked marks before the paper starts. Every heading says where it was asked.

subsections.heading: The atom, and what the numbers mean
subsections.html:
Spec 7.2, 7.3 · 2023 Q2(a)–(d) — six marks of multiple choice

A nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around it. Written as 146C:

  • The bottom number is the atomic (proton) number — the number of protons. It decides which element it is.
  • The top number is the mass (nucleon) number — protons + neutrons together.
  • Neutrons = top − bottom. For carbon-14: 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon — six protons each — but one has six neutrons and the other eight.

An ion is different again, and is about electrons: adding an electron makes a negative ion, removing one makes a positive ion. The nucleus is untouched.

subsections.heading: Why nuclei decay, and the three radiations
subsections.html:
Spec 7.4, 7.5 · Mock 2 Q4(b)

Some nuclei are unstable. They emit radiation from the nucleus, at random, to become more stable. All three types are ionising.

What it isStopped byIonising power
Alpha (α)2 protons + 2 neutrons — a helium nucleusA sheet of paper, or a few cm of airStrongly ionising
Beta (β−)A fast-moving electron from the nucleusA few mm of aluminiumModerately
Gamma (γ)A high-frequency electromagnetic waveThick lead or concrete — only reduced, never fully stoppedWeakly ionising

The pattern is worth noticing because it is the reason behind every application: the more strongly ionising a radiation is, the less far it penetrates. Alpha does its damage immediately and stops; gamma passes through almost everything precisely because it interacts so little.

Identifying an unknown source — the standard three marks

The count is unchanged by paper, but drops to background level with 5 mm of aluminium.

It is beta 1 — because paper does not reduce the count, so it is not alpha 1, and 5 mm of aluminium reduces it to background, so it is not gamma, which would penetrate 1.

Two of the three marks are for ruling the other two out. Naming the radiation alone scores one. Always write both eliminations.

subsections.heading: Ionisation
subsections.html:
Spec 7.4 · 2024 Q5(a)(ii)

Ionisation is the removal of electron(s) from an atom. That is the mark-scheme wording, and it is worth a mark on its own.

It matters because it is how radiation damages living things. An ionising particle rips electrons from the atoms it passes, which breaks molecules apart — including DNA — causing cell damage and mutations.

subsections.heading: Decay equations
subsections.html:
Spec 7.7, 7.8 · 2024 Q5(a)(i) · Mock 1 Q9(e)

Learn the effect of each emission on the two numbers:

EmissionMass numberAtomic number
AlphaDecreases by 4Decreases by 2
BetaUnchangedIncreases by 1
GammaUnchangedUnchanged
NeutronDecreases by 1Unchanged

Beta looks strange — the nucleus emits an electron and its proton count goes up. The reason: a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton, and the electron created is thrown out. So the total number of nucleons is the same, but one more of them is a proton.

Balancing is the whole technique: the top numbers must total the same on both sides, and so must the bottom numbers. For the beta decay of carbon-14:

146C → 147N + 0−1e

Top: 14 = 14 + 0 ✓. Bottom: 6 = 7 + (−1) ✓. The beta particle is written 0−1e — no nucleons, charge −1. An alpha particle is 42He.

subsections.heading: Background radiation
subsections.html:
Spec 7.10 · 2025 Q9(b) · Mock 2 Q4(a)

Ionising radiation that is present all the time, everywhere, even when no source is being used.

Sources: rocks and soil (especially granite), radon gas, cosmic rays from space, food and drink, and medical procedures such as X-rays.

2025's examiner penalised two specific things:

Do not use the word "background" inside the definition — "a number tried to use the word background in their answer which I didn't allow". Defining a term using itself explains nothing.

Do not say it comes only from natural sources — "A number of students were referring to the idea that it must come from natural sources, which I punished." Medical procedures and nuclear industry waste are part of it too.

subsections.heading: Activity and half-life
subsections.html:
Spec 7.11, 7.12 · 2024 Q5(b)(i) · 2025 Q9(c)(i) · Mock 1 Q9(b) — defined in two of three papers

Activity is the rate at which nuclei decay, measured in becquerels (Bq). One becquerel is one decay per second. Activity decreases over time, because there are fewer undecayed nuclei left to decay.

Half-life is the time taken for the activity of a sample — or the number of undecayed nuclei in it — to halve.

Both papers flag the same error: "The time for a nucleus to halve" scores zero. A single nucleus cannot halve. It either decays or it doesn't, and you cannot predict when.

The thing that halves is a property of the whole sample — its activity, its number of undecayed nuclei, or the mass of the isotope remaining. Say "of a sample" and the mark is safe.

subsections.heading: Half-life calculations — and the background trap
subsections.html:
Spec 7.13 · 2024 Q5(b)(ii) · 2025 Q9(c)(ii) · Mock 1 Q9(c) · Mock 2 Q4(d)

The method is repeated halving. Count how many halvings fit into the time, then halve that many times.

Worked example — activity after a given time

Initial activity 12 000 Bq, half-life 6.0 hours. What is the activity after 1 day?

1. Number of half-lives: 24 ÷ 6 = 4

2. Halve four times: 12 000 → 6000 → 3000 → 1500 → 750 Bq

Write the chain out. Mark schemes award a mark for the evidence of halving even if the final number slips.

Worked example — finding the half-life from a count rate

Background is 24 counts/min. With the source, the detector reads 424 counts/min. The corrected count rate falls to 50 counts/min after 96 minutes. Find the half-life.

1. Correct the initial reading for background. 424 − 24 = 400 counts/min. (The 50 is already corrected — read the question carefully to see which figures are which.)

2. Count the halvings: 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 is 3 half-lives

3. Divide: 96 ÷ 3 = 32 minutes

Subtract the background before you do anything else. Mock 2 is explicit: "Working from 424 gives a wrong number of half-lives and loses all three marks." The detector counts background whether the source is there or not, so the raw reading is not the source's activity.

From a graph: draw the lines. 2025 wanted "lines drawn on the graph from an activity to half that activity" — pick a starting activity, find where the curve reaches half of it, and read off the time difference. The construction lines are a mark.

And quote numbers. On the 2025 part asking candidates to test a relationship: "many candidates referred to the shape of the graph and tried to justify their answers without any data, which was awarded zero marks." Take readings off the graph and calculate with them.

subsections.heading: Randomness
subsections.html:
Spec 7.4 · 2023 Q2(e) · Mock 2 Q4(e)

Radioactive decay is a random process: it is impossible to predict when any individual nucleus will decay, and each has the same chance in a given time regardless of how long it has already existed.

Half-life is not a contradiction of this. With enormous numbers of nuclei, the average behaviour is highly predictable even though each individual event is not — in the same way that no one can say which particular people will make a phone call in the next minute, yet the total number of calls is very predictable.

subsections.heading: Uses, contamination and dangers
subsections.html:
Spec 7.14, 7.15, 7.16 · Mock 1 Q9(d) · 2024 Q5(a)(iii)

Every application follows from the penetration table. The exam asks you to justify a choice, so reason from the properties:

UseRadiationWhy
Medical tracerGammaPenetrating enough to escape the body and be detected; weakly ionising so it does least damage inside. Alpha would be absorbed within centimetres of tissue and never reach the detector, while ionising heavily on the way
Thickness monitoringBetaPartly absorbed by the sheet, so the count rate responds to thickness. Alpha would be stopped completely, gamma would pass through unaffected
Sterilising equipmentGammaPenetrates the sealed packaging to kill bacteria inside
Smoke detectorAlphaIonises the air to allow a small current; smoke blocks it. Short range makes it safe outside the device

Contamination versus irradiation — a distinction the specification names explicitly:

  • Irradiation is being exposed to radiation from a source outside you. It stops when you move away, and the object does not become radioactive.
  • Contamination is getting radioactive material on or inside you. It continues to irradiate you until it is removed or decays, which makes it the more serious.

Dangers and precautions: ionising radiation damages cells and tissue and can cause mutations. Reduce risk by keeping exposure times short, staying at a distance, and using shielding (lead, concrete) and remote handling tongs. Radioactive waste stays dangerous for a very long time and is sealed and stored securely, often deep underground.

subsections.heading: Fission and fusion
subsections.html:
Spec 7.17 – 7.26

Both release energy from the nucleus, and they are opposites:

FissionFusion
What happensA large nucleus (U-235) is split by a neutronSmall nuclei are joined into a larger one
ProductsTwo radioactive daughter nuclei, a few neutrons, and energy as kinetic energy of the fission productsA larger nucleus, with a loss of mass and a release of energy
WhereNuclear power stationsStars, including the Sun

Chain reaction: each fission releases neutrons, which can strike further U-235 nuclei and cause them to split too, so the process sustains itself.

In a reactor: control rods absorb neutrons to keep the rate steady — pushed in to slow it, withdrawn to speed it up. The moderator slows the neutrons down, because slow neutrons are far more likely to be absorbed and cause fission. Shielding — thick concrete and lead around the reactor — absorbs the radiation and protects the workers outside.

Why fusion needs stars: both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel each other electrostatically. Only at extremely high temperatures and pressures do they move fast enough to overcome that repulsion and get close enough to fuse — which is why it does not happen at everyday conditions.

subsections.heading: The definitions, word for word
subsections.html:
TermSay this
Half-lifeThe time taken for the activity of a sample to halve — or, the time taken for half the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay
ActivityThe number of nuclear decays per second, measured in becquerels (Bq)
IonisationThe removal of an electron from an atom, creating a charged ion
Background radiationThe ionising radiation that is present at all times, in the absence of any radioactive source being used
ContaminationRadioactive material getting onto or into an object or person
IrradiationBeing exposed to radiation from an external source, without becoming radioactive

Three specific rules from the 2025 report on this topic:

Half-life — it's the sample or the number of nuclei. Never "a nucleus". A single nucleus has no half-life; it either decays or it doesn't.

Background radiation — you cannot use the word "background" in the definition, and you must not say it is only natural. Some of it is artificial (medical, nuclear industry). Say: radiation present even when no source is being used.

Sources — acceptable named sources include rocks (especially granite, radon gas), cosmic rays from space, food and drink, and medical procedures. "Stars" was not credited.

subsections.heading: Half-life calculations
subsections.html:
Method — activity after n half-lives

  1. Number of half-lives = total time ÷ half-life
  2. Halve the starting activity that many times

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 6 days, after 24 days. 24 ÷ 6 = 4 half-lives. 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 Bq.

Method — finding half-life from a graph

  1. Pick a convenient starting activity on the curve
  2. Find where the activity has fallen to half that value
  3. The half-life is the time between those two points
  4. Check it by repeating from a different starting point — it should be the same

If the graph shows a background level, subtract it from all readings first. The curve should tend towards zero, not towards the background.

subsections.heading: Randomness, uses and dangers
subsections.html:
Radioactive decay is random — you cannot predict when any individual nucleus will decay. Half-life is a statistical average over an enormous number of nuclei, which is why it's reliable for a sample and meaningless for one atom.

UseWhich radiation and why
Smoke detectorAlpha — ionises air, and is stopped by smoke
Thickness control in a paper millBeta — partly absorbed, so the amount passing through indicates thickness
Sterilising equipment; killing cancer cellsGamma — penetrates packaging or the body
Medical tracersGamma, with a short half-life so it doesn't stay in the body

Dangers: radiation can damage cells and tissue, and can cause mutations in DNA which may lead to cancer. Radioactive waste stays hazardous for a very long time and must be sealed and stored securely, often deep underground.

subsections.heading: Fission and fusion
subsections.html:
FissionFusion
A large nucleus (U-235) splits into two smaller daughter nucleiTwo small nuclei join to form a larger one
Triggered by absorbing a slow-moving neutronRequires extremely high temperature and pressure
Releases 2–3 fast neutrons, which can cause a chain reactionNuclei must overcome the electrostatic repulsion between their protons
Used in nuclear power stations; produces radioactive wasteThe energy source of stars; produces no radioactive waste

In a reactor: the fuel rods contain enriched uranium. The moderator slows the fast neutrons so they can be absorbed by U-235. The control rods absorb excess neutrons to control the rate of the chain reaction. The shielding protects workers from the radiation emitted.

questions.promptHtml: Alpha radiation is the most dangerous of the three if the source is swallowed, but the least dangerous if the source is across the room. Explain this apparent contradiction.
questions.answerHtml:
Both facts follow from the same property: alpha is strongly ionising and weakly penetrating.

Across the room: alpha particles are absorbed by a few centimetres of air, and cannot penetrate the dead outer layer of your skin. Essentially none of the radiation reaches living tissue, so it does no harm.

Swallowed: the source is now inside, in direct contact with living cells. There's no air gap and no skin barrier. All that strong ionising power is deposited directly into tissue over a very short distance, causing intense localised damage to cells and DNA.

Gamma is the reverse: dangerous from outside because it penetrates, but less damaging per unit of exposure because it ionises weakly and much of it passes straight through.

questions.promptHtml: A sample has a half-life of 10 days. After 10 days half the nuclei have decayed. Why don't the remaining nuclei decay in the next 10 days, leaving none?
questions.answerHtml:
Because decay is random, not scheduled. Each surviving nucleus has the same probability of decaying in the next 10 days as it always had — about one in two. Nuclei do not age or "queue up".

So in the second 10 days, half of the remaining half decays, leaving a quarter. Then an eighth, then a sixteenth. Each half-life halves whatever is left, which is why the graph is a curve approaching zero rather than a straight line hitting it.

Consequence worth knowing: in principle the activity never reaches exactly zero. In practice it eventually drops below the background level and can't be distinguished from it.

questions.promptHtml: In beta decay, an electron is emitted from the nucleus. But the nucleus contains only protons and neutrons, and electrons orbit outside it. Where does the electron come from?
questions.answerHtml:
It doesn't come from the orbiting shells. It is created at the moment of decay, when a neutron inside the nucleus turns into a proton and an electron. The proton stays; the electron is ejected at high speed as the beta particle.

This explains the bookkeeping perfectly:

  • Mass number unchanged — one neutron became one proton, so the total nucleon count is the same
  • Atomic number increases by 1 — there is now one more proton, so it is a different element
  • Charge conserved — a neutral neutron became a +1 proton and a −1 electron, net zero

Nuclei emit beta radiation when they have too many neutrons relative to protons. Converting one to the other moves them towards stability.

questions.promptHtml: A medical tracer needs a short half-life. A smoke detector source needs a long one. Explain both, and identify what makes them opposite requirements.
questions.answerHtml:
Medical tracer — short half-life (hours). It must remain active long enough to be imaged, but decay quickly afterwards so the patient isn't exposed for longer than necessary. A long half-life would mean carrying a radioactive source around for years.

Smoke detector — long half-life (hundreds of years). It must keep working reliably for the whole life of the device without being replaced. A short half-life would mean the activity drops and the detector silently stops working.

The underlying trade-off: half-life determines how long a source stays useful and how long it stays hazardous. Where the source is inside a person, you want it gone fast. Where it's sealed inside a device that nobody touches, you want it to last.

The same reasoning explains why nuclear waste is such a problem: the isotopes that make good long-term fuel are exactly the ones that stay dangerous for millennia.

questions.promptHtml: "Half-life is the time taken for a nucleus to halve." This scores zero in every mark scheme. Why is it wrong — not just badly worded, but actually wrong?
questions.answerHtml:
Because a single nucleus cannot halve. It has only two possible states: undecayed, or decayed. There is no halfway. And decay is random, so it is impossible to predict when any particular nucleus will go.

What halves is a property of the whole sample. Any of these score:

  • the time taken for the activity of a sample to halve
  • the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei in a sample to halve
  • the time taken for the mass of the isotope remaining to halve

Why the average is predictable when the individual is not: there are astronomically many nuclei in any real sample. Each has a fixed probability of decaying in a given time, so the total number decaying per second is highly consistent — just as no one can say which individuals will phone in the next minute, yet the total number of calls is very predictable.

Two of the three past papers define half-life. Learn one of the three wordings above and write it verbatim.

questions.promptHtml: A detector reads 424 counts per minute with a source present, and 24 counts per minute with it removed. A student calculates half-lives starting from 424. Why does this lose every mark in the question?
questions.answerHtml:
Because 424 is not the activity of the source. It is the source plus the background radiation that is always present in the room.

The source's true contribution is 424 − 24 = 400 counts per minute. The background does not decay away, so it stays at 24 throughout while the source's contribution halves.

Why it destroys the whole answer: the halving chain from the wrong start never lands on the given values. From 400 you get a clean 400 → 200 → 100 → 50. From 424 you get 424 → 212 → 106 → 53, which matches nothing, so the number of half-lives is wrong and every subsequent figure follows it.

Mock 2: "Part (d) requires subtracting background first. Working from 424 gives a wrong number of half-lives and loses all three marks."

The habit: whenever a question mentions a background count at all, it is telling you to subtract it. It would not be there otherwise.

questions.promptHtml: Alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising but travels the shortest distance. Gamma is the least ionising and travels furthest. Why are these two properties linked, and what does it mean for choosing a source?
questions.answerHtml:
They are linked because ionising is how radiation loses energy. Every time a particle rips an electron off an atom, it gives up some of its own energy.

An alpha particle is large and highly charged, so it ionises very heavily — and therefore runs out of energy within a few centimetres of air. Gamma is an electromagnetic wave with no charge, so it interacts only rarely, keeps its energy, and travels a long way.

So the two properties are the same fact seen twice: heavy interaction means short range; light interaction means long range.

What it means for choosing a source:

  • Medical tracer → gamma. It must escape the body to be detected, and it should do minimal damage on the way. Alpha would be absorbed in the first few centimetres of tissue, never reach the detector, and cause serious cell damage while doing so.
  • Smoke detector → alpha. You need heavy ionisation of the air to produce a current, and the tiny range means it is harmless a few centimetres outside the device.
  • Thickness monitoring → beta. It must be partly absorbed by the sheet. Alpha would be stopped completely and gamma would pass through unchanged, so neither would respond to thickness.

questions.promptHtml: A nucleus emits a beta particle — an electron — and its atomic number goes up by one. How can throwing something out of the nucleus increase the proton count, when the nucleus contains no electrons to begin with?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the electron is created at the moment of decay, not stored and released.

Inside the nucleus, a neutron turns into a proton. Doing so produces an electron, which is immediately ejected — that is the beta particle.

Follow the bookkeeping:

  • Neutron count falls by one, proton count rises by one. Total nucleons unchanged, so the mass number stays the same.
  • One extra proton means the atomic number rises by one — it is now a different element.
  • Charge is conserved: a neutral neutron became a positive proton plus a negative electron. Which is why the beta particle is written 0−1e, and why the bottom numbers balance as 6 = 7 + (−1).

Contrast with alpha, which really is a chunk of the nucleus leaving: two protons and two neutrons, so mass number down 4 and atomic number down 2.

questions.promptHtml: Being irradiated and being contaminated both expose you to radiation. Which is more serious, and why does the distinction matter practically?
questions.answerHtml:
Contamination is more serious.

Irradiation means radiation from a source outside you reaches your body. Move away, or put shielding in between, and it stops immediately. The object being irradiated does not become radioactive itself — which is why irradiated food is perfectly safe to eat.

Contamination means radioactive material has got onto or into you. The source is now travelling with you, so it keeps irradiating you until it is physically removed or decays away. You cannot walk away from it.

Why it changes the danger from each type: the ranking reverses. Outside the body, alpha is the least dangerous — it cannot even penetrate skin — while gamma is the worst because it reaches your organs. Inside the body, alpha is by far the worst, because all of its heavy ionising power is delivered directly into living tissue with nothing to absorb it first.

Practically: irradiation is handled with distance, shielding and short exposure times. Contamination is handled by preventing contact altogether — gloves, sealed sources, remote handling tongs.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why workers in a room containing an alpha source are not at risk, but would be at risk from a gamma source of the same activity. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Alpha particles are absorbed by a few centimetres of air 1, and cannot penetrate skin, so they do not reach living tissue 1

Gamma rays are highly penetrating, so they pass through air and into the body where they can ionise atoms and damage cells 1

markScheme.point: Alpha particles are absorbed by a few centimetres of air , and cannot penetrate skin, so they do not reach living tissue
Gamma rays are highly penetrating, so they pass through air and into the body where they can ionise atoms and damage cells

questions.promptHtml: Explain the difference between contamination and irradiation, and state which is generally more dangerous over the long term. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Irradiation is exposure to radiation from a source outside the body; the object or person does not become radioactive 1

Contamination is radioactive material getting onto or into the object or person, so it remains there and continues to emit radiation 1

Contamination is generally more dangerous long term, because exposure continues after the person leaves the area and cannot simply be stopped by moving away or shielding 1

markScheme.point: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from a source outside the body; the object or person does not become radioactive
Contamination is radioactive material getting onto or into the object or person, so it remains there and continues to emit radiation
Contamination is generally more dangerous long term, because exposure continues after the person leaves the area and cannot simply be stopped by moving away or shielding

questions.promptHtml:
A student uses a Geiger–Müller detector to investigate a radioactive source. Before the source is introduced, the detector records 22 counts per minute.

(a) Explain what this reading is, and give two sources of it. (3)
(b) With the source present the detector reads 342 counts per minute. This is unchanged by a sheet of paper, but falls to 22 counts per minute with a 5 mm aluminium sheet. Identify the radiation and justify your answer. (3)
(c) State what happens to the atomic number and the mass number when a nucleus emits this radiation. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Background radiation — ionising radiation present all the time, even when no source is being used 1

Any two named sources 11: rocks and soil · radon gas · cosmic rays from space · food and drink · medical procedures

(b) Beta 1

Paper does not reduce the count, so it is not alpha 1

5 mm of aluminium reduces it to the background level, so it is not gamma, which would penetrate 1

(c) Mass number unchanged 1 · atomic number increases by 1 1

In (a), do not use the word "background" inside the definition, and do not say it comes only from natural sources — 2025 penalised both. In (b), two of the three marks are for ruling out the other radiations. Naming beta alone scores one.

markScheme.point: (a) Background radiation — ionising radiation present all the time, even when no source is being used
Any two named sources : rocks and soil · radon gas · cosmic rays from space · food and drink · medical procedures
(b) Beta
Paper does not reduce the count, so it is not alpha
5 mm of aluminium reduces it to the background level, so it is not gamma, which would penetrate
(c) Mass number unchanged · atomic number increases by 1

questions.promptHtml:
(a) State what is meant by the half-life of a radioactive source. (2)
(b) A source has an initial activity of 9600 Bq and a half-life of 8.0 hours. Calculate its activity after 32 hours. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The time taken 1 for the activity of a sample, or the number of undecayed nuclei in it, to halve 1

(b) Number of half-lives = 32 ÷ 8.0 = 4 1

9600 → 4800 → 2400 → 1200 → 600 1

= 600 Bq 1

"The time for a nucleus to halve" scores zero. A single nucleus cannot halve — it either decays or it does not. Say of a sample.

Write the halving chain out. There is a mark for evidence of halving even if the final number slips.

markScheme.point: (a) The time taken for the activity of a sample, or the number of undecayed nuclei in it, to halve
(b) Number of half-lives = 32 ÷ 8.0 = 4

questions.promptHtml:
A detector records 22 counts per minute with no source present. With a source in place it reads 822 counts per minute. After 75 minutes the corrected count rate has fallen to 100 counts per minute.

Determine the half-life of the source. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Corrected initial count = 822 − 22 = 800 counts per minute 1

800 → 400 → 200 → 100 is 3 half-lives 1

Half-life = 75 ÷ 3 = 25 minutes 1

Subtract the background first. Mock 2: "Working from [the uncorrected figure] gives a wrong number of half-lives and loses all three marks." The background does not decay — it stays constant while the source's contribution halves.

Whenever a question tells you a background count, it is telling you to subtract it. It would not be mentioned otherwise.

markScheme.point: Corrected initial count = 822 − 22 = 800 counts per minute
Half-life = 75 ÷ 3 = 25 minutes

questions.promptHtml:
Complete the following decay equations, and name the type of decay in each case. (6)

(a) 22688Ra → ______Rn + 42He
(b) 146C → ______N + 0−1e
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 22286Rn 11 — alpha decay 1

Mass number falls by 4 (226 − 4 = 222); atomic number falls by 2 (88 − 2 = 86).

(b) 147N 11 — beta decay 1

Mass number unchanged; atomic number rises by 1 (6 → 7).

Check both lines every time. Top: 14 = 14 + 0 ✓. Bottom: 6 = 7 + (−1) ✓. The beta particle's atomic number of −1 is what makes the bottom line balance, and forgetting the minus sign is the usual error.

markScheme.point: (a) 22286Rn — alpha decay
(b) 147N — beta decay

questions.promptHtml:
A hospital uses a gamma-emitting source as a medical tracer.

(a) State the unit of activity. (1)
(b) Explain why gamma radiation is more suitable than alpha for this purpose. (3)
(c) Suggest why a source with a half-life of several years would be unsuitable. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The becquerel (Bq) 1

(b) Gamma is highly penetrating, so it can pass out of the body to be detected 1

Alpha would be absorbed within a few centimetres of tissue and never reach the detector 1

Alpha is also strongly ionising, so it would cause serious damage to cells inside the body 1

(c) The source would remain active inside the patient long after the scan 1

continuing to irradiate their tissue for years and increasing the risk of cell damage or mutation, with no medical benefit 1

Tracers use short half-lives — hours, not years — for exactly this reason. The activity must last long enough for the scan and then fall away quickly.

markScheme.point: (a) The becquerel (Bq)
(b) Gamma is highly penetrating, so it can pass out of the body to be detected
Alpha would be absorbed within a few centimetres of tissue and never reach the detector
Alpha is also strongly ionising, so it would cause serious damage to cells inside the body
(c) The source would remain active inside the patient long after the scan
continuing to irradiate their tissue for years and increasing the risk of cell damage or mutation, with no medical benefit

questions.promptHtml:
(a) State what is meant by ionisation. (1)
(b) Explain why ionising radiation is dangerous to living cells. (2)
(c) Describe two ways a worker handling a radioactive source can reduce their exposure. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The removal of electron(s) from an atom 1

(b) The radiation removes electrons from atoms in the cell, which breaks up molecules including DNA 1

This damages cells and tissue, and can cause mutations which may lead to cancer 1

(c) Any two 11: keep exposure times short · stay as far from the source as possible · use shielding such as lead or concrete · handle the source with remote tongs rather than by hand · store it in a lead-lined container when not in use

markScheme.point: (a) The removal of electron(s) from an atom
(b) The radiation removes electrons from atoms in the cell, which breaks up molecules including DNA
This damages cells and tissue, and can cause mutations which may lead to cancer

(c) Any two : keep exposure times short · stay as far from the source as possible · use shielding such as lead or concrete · handle the source with remote tongs rather than by hand · store it in a lead-lined container when not in use

questions.promptHtml: Explain the difference between contamination and irradiation, and state which is the more serious. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Irradiation is exposure to radiation from a source that is outside the body 1

It stops as soon as the source is removed or you move away, and the irradiated object does not become radioactive 1

Contamination is radioactive material getting onto or inside the body 1

Contamination is more serious, because the source stays with the person and continues to irradiate them until it is removed or decays 1

Note that the ranking of the three radiations reverses between the two cases. Outside the body gamma is the most dangerous and alpha the least, because alpha cannot penetrate skin. Inside the body alpha is by far the worst, because its heavy ionisation is delivered straight into living tissue.

markScheme.point: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from a source that is outside the body
It stops as soon as the source is removed or you move away, and the irradiated object does not become radioactive
Contamination is radioactive material getting onto or inside the body
Contamination is more serious, because the source stays with the person and continues to irradiate them until it is removed or decays

questions.promptHtml:
(a) Describe the process of nuclear fission of a uranium-235 nucleus. (3)
(b) Explain how a chain reaction can occur. (2)
(c) Describe the roles of the control rods and the moderator in a nuclear reactor. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) A neutron collides with the U-235 nucleus and is absorbed 1

The nucleus splits into two radioactive daughter nuclei and a small number of neutrons 1

Energy is released, mainly as the kinetic energy of the fission products 1

(b) The neutrons released by one fission can strike other U-235 nuclei 1

causing them to split as well, so the reaction sustains itself 1

(c) Control rods absorb neutrons 1, and are lowered further in to slow the reaction or withdrawn to speed it up, keeping the rate steady 1

The moderator slows the neutrons down, because slow neutrons are much more likely to be absorbed and cause further fission 1

Shielding is a separate idea: thick concrete and lead around the reactor absorb the radiation and protect the workers outside.

markScheme.point: (a) A neutron collides with the U-235 nucleus and is absorbed
The nucleus splits into two radioactive daughter nuclei and a small number of neutrons
Energy is released, mainly as the kinetic energy of the fission products
(b) The neutrons released by one fission can strike other U-235 nuclei
causing them to split as well, so the reaction sustains itself
(c) Control rods absorb neutrons , and are lowered further in to slow the reaction or withdrawn to speed it up, keeping the rate steady
The moderator slows the neutrons down, because slow neutrons are much more likely to be absorbed and cause further fission

questions.promptHtml:
(a) Explain the difference between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission. (3)
(b) Explain why nuclear fusion does not occur at low temperatures and pressures. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) In fission a large nucleus is split into two smaller nuclei 1

In fusion two small nuclei are joined together to create a larger nucleus 1

Both release energy; fusion does so through a loss of mass, and it is the energy source of stars 1

(b) Both nuclei are positively charged 1

so they repel each other electrostatically 1

Only at very high temperatures and pressures do they move fast enough to overcome this repulsion and get close enough to fuse 1

The word the mark scheme wants is electrostatic repulsion — between the positive charges. "They push each other away" without naming why scores less.

markScheme.point: (a) In fission a large nucleus is split into two smaller nuclei
In fusion two small nuclei are joined together to create a larger nucleus
Both release energy; fusion does so through a loss of mass, and it is the energy source of stars
(b) Both nuclei are positively charged
so they repel each other electrostatically
Only at very high temperatures and pressures do they move fast enough to overcome this repulsion and get close enough to fuse

questions.promptHtml: Explain why radioactive decay is described as a random process, and how this is consistent with a source having a predictable half-life. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
It is impossible to predict when any individual nucleus will decay 1

Each nucleus has the same chance of decaying in a given time, regardless of how long it has already existed 1

A real sample contains an enormous number of nuclei, so although each individual event is unpredictable, the average behaviour of the whole sample is highly consistent — which is why the half-life is a reliable, repeatable quantity 1

The two ideas are not in tension. Nobody can say which individuals will make a phone call in the next minute, yet the total number of calls made is very predictable.

markScheme.point: It is impossible to predict when any individual nucleus will decay
Each nucleus has the same chance of decaying in a given time, regardless of how long it has already existed

A real sample contains an enormous number of nuclei, so although each individual event is unpredictable, the average behaviour of the whole sample is highly consistent — which is why the half-life is a reliable, repeatable quantity

questions.promptHtml:
A radioactive isotope has the symbol 9038Sr.

(a) State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of this isotope. (3)
(b) Another isotope of the same element is 8838Sr. Explain what makes these two isotopes. (2)
(c) Explain how a neutral atom becomes a negative ion. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Protons = 38 1 · neutrons = 90 − 38 = 52 1 · electrons = 38, equal to the protons in a neutral atom 1

(b) They have the same number of protons — both are strontium 1

but different numbers of neutrons (52 and 50) 1

(c) By gaining one or more electrons 1

Ions are about electrons; isotopes are about neutrons. Both were tested in the same multiple-choice question in 2023, and confusing them is easy under pressure.

markScheme.point: (a) Protons = 38 · neutrons = 90 − 38 = 52 · electrons = 38, equal to the protons in a neutral atom
(b) They have the same number of protons — both are strontium
but different numbers of neutrons (52 and 50)
(c) By gaining one or more electrons

modules.title: Practical and Data Skills
modules.standfirst: Not a topic — a set of marks scattered through every paper. Roughly one mark in eleven, requiring no physics knowledge at all, and routinely thrown away.

intel.html:
PaperWhat was asked
2023 Q7 (13)Describe a method for a projectile investigation, curve of best fit, read a value from a graph, justify line graph over bar chart, use graph data to verify a formula
2023 Q4b (2)Plot results, draw a curve of best fit, suggest an improvement
2024 Q2b, Q6a (9)Describe how to find mass and volume; describe an investigation to find specific heat capacity
2025 Q8 (10)Independent and dependent variables, two improvements to validity, improving reliability, plot a bar chart, justify bar over line

These marks are available regardless of whether you can do the physics. A student who has forgotten every equation can still take most of them.

2023: "Most answers were too vague here to pick up this mark. Repeats or collect more measurements / take more readings is too vague."

2023: "Common error was missing off (0.0,0.0) or using dots for plots that were so small I couldn't actually see all of them. Please encourage students to use X or bigger dots — their papers will get scanned for actual GCSE and I would worry that some would get missed."

2025: "some awful scales which made it easy to plot 90/180 but difficult to plot the 240/140 lines... lots of students not labelling the axes." And on justifying the chart type: "This was answered poorly - I was holding out specifically for the right vocab."

2025 on improving validity: "the question specifically says 'what can be done to improve' and some students lost marks by just saying e.g. the rods aren't the same length."

That last one is a general rule worth internalising: if the question says "improve", your answer must be an instruction, not an observation. Not "the rods are different lengths" but "use rods of the same length".
